entries.title: Big Bang
entries.mainstream: The observable universe expanded from a hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago, supported by the cosmic microwave background, light-element abundances and galaxy redshifts.

alternatives.label: Alternative cosmologies
alternatives.text: Steady-state, cyclic/bouncing and other models have been proposed; steady-state lost support after the 1965 discovery of the CMB, while cyclic models remain theoretical proposals.

entries.changed: 1920s: Lemaître and Hubble show expansion. 1965: CMB discovered, steady-state model largely abandoned. 2013–2018: Planck refines age to ~13.8 Gyr.

media.title: Why the Big Bang Definitely Happened | Space Time | PBS Digital Studios

entries.title: Formation of the Earth
entries.mainstream: Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago, dated from meteorites and the oldest terrestrial minerals.

alternatives.label: Young-Earth creationism
alternatives.text: Some religious readings hold the Earth is thousands of years old; this is rejected by mainstream geology.

entries.changed: 17th c.: Ussher dates creation to 4004 BCE. 19th c.: geologists argue for vast ages; Kelvin estimates 20–400 Myr. 1956: Patterson obtains ~4.55 Gyr from meteorite lead isotopes.

sources.title: The age of the Earth in the twentieth century: a problem (mostly) solved

entries.title: Great Oxidation Event
entries.mainstream: Oxygen produced by cyanobacteria began accumulating in the atmosphere about 2.4 billion years ago.

entries.title: Cambrian explosion
entries.mainstream: Rapid diversification of animal body plans in the fossil record beginning about 539 million years ago.

alternatives.label: Artefact of preservation
alternatives.text: Some researchers argue the apparent suddenness partly reflects earlier, poorly fossilised ancestors (molecular clocks suggest older origins).

entries.title: End-Cretaceous extinction (dinosaurs)
entries.mainstream: A large asteroid impact at Chicxulub, Mexico, is widely accepted as the main cause of the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs 66 million years ago.

alternatives.label: Deccan Traps volcanism
alternatives.text: Some geologists argue massive Indian volcanism was a major or co-equal cause.

entries.changed: 1980: Alvarez team proposes impact from iridium anomaly, initially controversial. 1991: Chicxulub crater identified; impact becomes mainstream.

sources.title: Extraterrestrial Cause for the Cretaceous-Tertiary Extinction

media.title: How We Figured Out an Asteroid Killed the Dinosaurs

entries.title: Dragons, griffins and fossil finds
entries.mainstream: Dragon and griffin legends appear across many cultures. Historian Adrienne Mayor proposed that ancient discoveries of fossils (e.g. Protoceratops for the griffin) inspired some of them.

alternatives.label: Critique
alternatives.text: A 2024 study argued the Protoceratops–griffin link is not supported by the evidence.

alternatives.label: Living-dinosaur claims
alternatives.text: Some creationist writers claim dragon legends record humans living with dinosaurs; mainstream science rejects this (66 Myr gap).

sources.title: Did the horned dinosaur Protoceratops inspire the griffin?

entries.title: Earliest Homo species
entries.mainstream: The earliest fossils assigned to the genus Homo date to about 2.8 million years ago in East Africa.

entries.title: Earliest Homo sapiens (Jebel Irhoud)
entries.mainstream: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, dated to about 300,000 years ago, are the earliest attributed to Homo sapiens.
entries.changed: Before 2017, the oldest H. sapiens fossils were ~195 kyr (Omo Kibish, Ethiopia); Jebel Irhoud pushed it back and suggested a pan-African origin.

sources.title: New fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco and the pan-African origin of Homo sapiens

entries.title: Toba supereruption
entries.mainstream: A very large eruption of Toba (Sumatra) occurred ~74,000 years ago. Its effect on humans is debated.

alternatives.label: Toba catastrophe theory
alternatives.text: Proposes a volcanic winter caused a human population bottleneck.

alternatives.label: Limited impact
alternatives.text: Lake Malawi sediments show no major cooling in East Africa.

sources.title: Ash from the Toba supereruption in Lake Malawi shows no volcanic winter in East Africa at 75 ka

media.title: How a Supervolcano Ignited an Evolutionary Debate

entries.title: Neanderthal & Denisovan interbreeding
entries.mainstream: Genome studies show modern non-African humans carry some Neanderthal DNA, and some populations carry Denisovan DNA.
entries.changed: Long debated whether Neanderthals and modern humans interbred; the 2010 Neanderthal draft genome showed they did. 2010: Denisovans identified from DNA alone.

sources.title: A Draft Sequence of the Neandertal Genome
The complete mitochondrial DNA genome of an unknown hominin from southern Siberia

media.title: The Ancient Human Species With A Missing Body

entries.title: Sulawesi cave art
entries.mainstream: Painted hunting scenes in Sulawesi, Indonesia, dated to at least ~44,000 years ago (later finds older still).
entries.changed: Until the 2010s, Europe was widely assumed to be the cradle of figurative cave art.

sources.title: Earliest hunting scene in prehistoric art

entries.title: Chauvet Cave paintings
entries.mainstream: Cave paintings in southern France, among the oldest known figurative art in Europe (~36,000 years ago).

sources.title: A high-precision chronological model for the decorated Upper Paleolithic cave of Chauvet-Pont d’Arc, Ardèche, France

entries.title: Peopling of the Americas
entries.mainstream: Humans were in the Americas by at least ~16,000 years ago; footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, have been dated to ~21,000–23,000 years ago, though some dispute those dates.

alternatives.label: Clovis first
alternatives.text: The once-dominant view that Clovis people (~13,000 years ago) were first; now largely abandoned.

entries.changed: "Clovis first" dominated mid-20th c.; Monte Verde (Chile) accepted ~1997 as pre-Clovis; 2021 White Sands footprints push dates further back.

sources.title: Evidence of humans in North America during the Last Glacial Maximum

entries.title: Meltwater Pulse 1A (rapid sea-level rise)
entries.mainstream: At the end of the last Ice Age, sea level rose roughly 14–18 m in a few centuries around 14,600 years ago.

alternatives.label: Link to flood myths
alternatives.text: Some authors propose post-glacial sea-level rise is remembered in flood myths (speculative).

sources.title: Ice-sheet collapse and sea-level rise at the Bølling warming 14,600 years ago

entries.title: Younger Dryas cold interval
entries.mainstream: An abrupt return to near-glacial conditions in the Northern Hemisphere (~12,900–11,700 years ago), well recorded in Greenland ice cores; commonly attributed to disruption of North Atlantic ocean circulation.

alternatives.label: Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis
alternatives.text: Proposes a cosmic impact or airburst ~12,900 years ago contributed to the cooling and megafaunal extinctions; contested. Some popular authors link it to global flood myths (speculative).

sources.title: The Younger Dryas cold interval as viewed from central Greenland
Evidence for an extraterrestrial impact 12,900 years ago that contributed to the megafaunal extinctions and the Younger Dryas cooling
The Younger Dryas impact hypothesis: a cosmic catastrophe

media.title: When the Earth Suddenly Stopped Warming

entries.title: Ice Age lost civilisation hypothesis
entries.mainstream: Mainstream archaeology finds no evidence of an advanced civilisation during the last Ice Age.

alternatives.label: Lost advanced civilisation
alternatives.text: Writers such as Graham Hancock propose an advanced Ice Age civilisation destroyed around the Younger Dryas, whose knowledge survived in myths and monuments.

entries.title: Göbekli Tepe
entries.mainstream: Pre-Pottery Neolithic monumental site in SE Türkiye with carved T-shaped pillars, built by hunter-gatherer communities; UNESCO World Heritage Site.

alternatives.label: Astronomical / catastrophe readings
alternatives.text: Some researchers and authors interpret pillar carvings as astronomical records, including of a Younger Dryas-era impact; these readings are disputed by excavators (speculative).

entries.changed: Surveyed in 1963 and thought to be a medieval cemetery; excavations from 1995 (Klaus Schmidt) revealed its Neolithic age.

sources.title: Göbekli Tepe, Southeastern Turkey. A Preliminary Report on the 1995-1999 Excavations.

media.title: Stone Age Temple Mystery | Full Documentary | NOVA | PBS

entries.title: Drowning of Sundaland
entries.mainstream: Post-glacial sea-level rise flooded the Sunda Shelf of Southeast Asia, which had been a large land area during the Ice Age.

alternatives.label: Cradle of civilisation
alternatives.text: Stephen Oppenheimer ("Eden in the East") proposed Sundaland as a source of later cultures and flood myths; not widely accepted.

entries.title: Aboriginal stories of coastal drowning
entries.mainstream: Aboriginal Australian oral traditions from many coastal areas describe land lost to the sea; Nunn & Reid argue some may preserve memories of post-glacial sea-level rise >7,000 years ago.

alternatives.label: Caution
alternatives.text: Others note the difficulty of dating oral traditions and the possibility of later reinterpretation.

sources.title: Aboriginal Memories of Inundation of the Australian Coast Dating from More than 7000 Years Ago

entries.title: Doggerland flooded / Storegga tsunami
entries.mainstream: The North Sea plain linking Britain to Europe was progressively flooded; the Storegga Slide tsunami (~6200 BCE) struck its remaining lowlands.

alternatives.label: Extent debated
alternatives.text: How much of Doggerland remained when the tsunami hit is debated.

sources.title: The catastrophic final flooding of Doggerland by the Storegga Slide tsunami

media.author: James Walker, Vincent Gaffney,Simon Fitch,Merle Muru, Andrew Fraser, Martin Bates and Richard Bates

entries.title: Black Sea deluge hypothesis
entries.mainstream: Ryan and Pitman proposed an abrupt flooding of the Black Sea from the Mediterranean around 5600 BCE.

alternatives.label: Gradual reconnection
alternatives.text: Other studies argue for a gradual or smaller rise.

alternatives.label: Flood-myth source
alternatives.text: Proposers linked the event to Near Eastern flood stories; disputed.

sources.title: An abrupt drowning of the Black Sea shelf

entries.title: Çatalhöyük
entries.mainstream: A large Neolithic settlement in Anatolia, among the best-preserved early farming towns.

entries.title: Invention of writing (Mesopotamia)
entries.mainstream: Cuneiform developed in Sumer around 3200 BCE; Egyptian hieroglyphs appear at a similar time.

entries.title: Stonehenge
entries.mainstream: A Neolithic and Bronze Age monument in England built in several phases; aligned on solstice sunrise/sunset.

alternatives.label: Folklore
alternatives.text: Medieval legend (Geoffrey of Monmouth) credited Merlin with moving the stones from Ireland.

entries.title: Great Pyramid of Giza
entries.mainstream: Built as the tomb of the Fourth Dynasty king Khufu, c. 2600–2500 BCE; radiocarbon dates on mortar broadly support an Old Kingdom date.

alternatives.label: Older or non-dynastic origin
alternatives.text: Alternative authors propose much older construction or a lost advanced civilisation; these claims lack support in peer-reviewed archaeology (speculative).

sources.title: Radiocarbon Dates of Old and Middle Kingdom Monuments in Egypt
Memphis and its Necropolis – the Pyramid Fields from Giza to Dahshur (UNESCO)

media.title: How did they build the Great Pyramid of Giza? - Soraya Field Fiorio

entries.title: Sphinx water-erosion hypothesis
entries.mainstream: Egyptologists date the Great Sphinx to Khafre's reign (~2500 BCE).

alternatives.label: Older Sphinx
alternatives.text: Geologist Robert Schoch argued weathering of the enclosure implies heavy rainfall and a much older date (pre-dynastic); most geologists and Egyptologists disagree.

sources.title: Seismic investigations in the vicinity of the great Sphinx of Giza, Egypt

entries.title: Flood narrative: Epic of Gilgamesh (Utnapishtim)
entries.dateNote: Standard Babylonian version c. 1200 BCE; older Mesopotamian flood stories (Atrahasis) earlier
entries.mainstream: A Mesopotamian literary flood story, widely seen as related to the Genesis account; often linked to local river floods.

alternatives.label: Memory of a real event
alternatives.text: Some propose it preserves memory of a large flood (e.g. Black Sea or post-glacial sea-level rise); not established.

entries.changed: 1872: George Smith identified the flood tablet in the British Museum, sparking debate on Genesis origins.

entries.title: Great Flood of Gun-Yu (China)
entries.mainstream: Chinese tradition says Yu the Great tamed a great flood and founded the Xia dynasty. A 2016 study linked it to a landslide-dam outburst flood on the Yellow River c. 1920 BCE.

alternatives.label: Critique
alternatives.text: A 2017 comment disputed the dating and its link to the Xia.

sources.title: Outburst flood at 1920 BCE supports historicity of China’s Great Flood and the Xia dynasty
Comment on “Outburst flood at 1920 BCE supports historicity of China’s Great Flood and the Xia dynasty”

entries.title: Minoan eruption of Thera
entries.mainstream: A massive eruption of Santorini in the late 17th or 16th century BCE; dating is debated between radiocarbon and archaeological chronologies.

alternatives.label: Atlantis inspiration
alternatives.text: Some propose the eruption and the Minoan civilisation inspired Plato's Atlantis story (hypothesis).

sources.title: Santorini Eruption Radiocarbon Dated to 1627-1600 B.C.

entries.title: The Exodus
entries.mainstream: Most historians and archaeologists consider the biblical Exodus narrative not historical as described; some propose a smaller historical core.

alternatives.label: Historical event
alternatives.text: Some scholars and religious traditions maintain a historical Exodus, with various proposed dates.

entries.title: Late Bronze Age collapse
entries.mainstream: Widespread collapse of Eastern Mediterranean states around 1200–1150 BCE, with causes including drought, earthquakes, invasions (Sea Peoples) and systems failure debated.

media.title: 2. The Bronze Age Collapse - Mediterranean Apocalypse

entries.title: Troy
entries.mainstream: The city of Homer's Iliad is widely identified with the site of Hisarlik in Türkiye, destroyed around 1180 BCE. Whether a "Trojan War" as described occurred is debated.

alternatives.label: Pure myth
alternatives.text: Earlier scholars viewed Troy as purely legendary.

entries.changed: Long considered legendary; 1870s excavations (Calvert, Schliemann) at Hisarlik revealed a multi-layered city.

media.title: 2. The Bronze Age Collapse - Mediterranean Apocalypse

entries.title: Flood narrative: Genesis 6–9 (Noah)
entries.dateNote: Composition date debated; often placed mid-1st millennium BCE
entries.mainstream: Hebrew Bible flood story; scholars note close parallels with Mesopotamian accounts.

alternatives.label: Literal global flood
alternatives.text: Some religious traditions read it as a historical worldwide flood.

alternatives.label: Black Sea hypothesis
alternatives.text: Ryan and Pitman linked a proposed Black Sea flood to flood traditions; debated.

entries.title: Flood narrative: Manu and the fish (Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1)
entries.dateNote: Text dated roughly early-mid 1st millennium BCE
entries.mainstream: Vedic prose account in which a fish warns Manu of a flood; later expanded in Puranic matsya stories.

alternatives.label: Shared deep memory
alternatives.text: Some argue flood myths across cultures reflect common post-glacial events; others see independent local origins (speculative).

entries.title: Flood narrative: Deucalion (Greek)
entries.mainstream: Greek myth in which Zeus floods the world and Deucalion and Pyrrha survive in a chest/ark; told by Apollodorus and Ovid.

entries.title: Atlantis (Plato)
entries.mainstream: Plato's dialogues Timaeus and Critias (c. 360 BCE) describe Atlantis, said to have sunk 9,000 years before Solon. Most scholars regard it as a philosophical allegory invented by Plato.

alternatives.label: Real place
alternatives.text: Many proposed locations (Thera/Minoan Crete, Atlantic, Antarctica, others); none accepted by mainstream scholarship.

alternatives.label: Ice Age memory
alternatives.text: Some alternative authors link it to the Younger Dryas and sea-level rise (speculative).

entries.title: Book of Enoch (1 Enoch)
entries.mainstream: Jewish apocalyptic work composed in sections c. 3rd–1st century BCE; Aramaic fragments found among the Dead Sea Scrolls; canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.

alternatives.label: Watchers as historical
alternatives.text: Some alternative authors read the Watchers/Nephilim narrative as a record of real non-human or advanced beings (speculative).

entries.changed: Known in the West mainly by quotation until James Bruce brought Ethiopic copies to Europe in 1773; Qumran fragments found from 1947.

sources.title: The Book of Enoch, tr. R.H. Charles, 1917

entries.title: Antikythera mechanism
entries.mainstream: A Greek geared astronomical calculator (c. 2nd–1st century BCE) recovered from a shipwreck in 1901.

alternatives.label: Out-of-place artefact
alternatives.text: Sometimes cited in alternative literature as evidence of lost technology; researchers regard it as Hellenistic Greek engineering.

entries.changed: Largely misunderstood until X-ray and CT studies (Price 1970s; Freeth et al. 2006) revealed its function.

sources.title: Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism

media.title: Antikythera Mechanism Part 1: by Nature Video

entries.title: Popol Vuh (K'iche' Maya)
entries.mainstream: K'iche' Maya text recording creation stories, including earlier failed creations of humans destroyed by flood; written down in the 16th century from older traditions.

entries.title: Pangu creation myth (China)
entries.mainstream: Chinese myth in which Pangu separates heaven and earth; first recorded by Xu Zheng in the 3rd century CE.

entries.title: Norse mythology: Ragnarök
entries.dateNote: Recorded in the Poetic and Prose Eddas, 13th century
entries.mainstream: Norse myths of the end and renewal of the world, recorded in 13th-century Icelandic sources.

alternatives.label: Climate memory
alternatives.text: Some researchers suggest the "Fimbulwinter" motif may recall the 536 CE volcanic cooling (hypothesis).

entries.title: Vikings in Vinland (L'Anse aux Meadows)
entries.mainstream: Norse sagas describe voyages to "Vinland". The site at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland, confirms a Norse presence; tree-ring evidence dates woodcutting there to 1021 CE.
entries.changed: Sagas long treated as uncertain legend; site excavated 1960s (Ingstad); exact date fixed in 2021.

sources.title: Evidence for European presence in the Americas in ad 1021

entries.title: King Arthur
entries.mainstream: Legendary British king; most historians consider a historical Arthur unproven, with the legend developed largely in later medieval literature.

alternatives.label: Historical figure
alternatives.text: Some argue for a real 5th–6th-century war leader behind the legend.

entries.title: Shroud of Turin
entries.mainstream: 1988 radiocarbon dating by three laboratories placed the linen at 1260–1390 CE.

alternatives.label: Authentic burial cloth
alternatives.text: Some researchers and believers dispute the sampling and hold it to be the burial cloth of Jesus.

sources.title: Radiocarbon dating of the Shroud of Turin

entries.title: Gutenberg printing press
entries.mainstream: Movable-type printing in Europe spread rapidly after c. 1450, transforming the circulation of knowledge (movable type existed earlier in China and Korea).

entries.title: Heliocentrism and Galileo
entries.mainstream: Copernicus published a Sun-centred model in 1543; Galileo's telescopic observations supported it, and he was tried by the Inquisition in 1633.
entries.changed: Geocentrism dominated for ~1,500 years; heliocentrism accepted by the late 17th century. The Catholic Church formally acknowledged errors in the Galileo case in 1992.

entries.title: Tunguska event
entries.mainstream: A large airburst flattened ~2,000 km² of Siberian forest in 1908, generally attributed to an asteroid or comet fragment.

alternatives.label: Other explanations
alternatives.text: Many alternative explanations have been proposed (e.g. natural gas, exotic physics); none accepted.

entries.title: Piltdown Man hoax
entries.mainstream: Fossils "found" in England in 1912 were presented as a missing link; exposed in 1953 as a forgery made from a human skull and an orangutan jaw.
entries.changed: 1912–1953: accepted by many British scientists. 1953: exposed by Weiner, Oakley and Le Gros Clark. 2016: DNA and morphology analysis suggests a single hoaxer, probably Charles Dawson.

sources.title: New genetic and morphological evidence suggests a single hoaxer created ‘Piltdown man’

entries.title: Continental drift / plate tectonics accepted
entries.mainstream: Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912; it was widely rejected until seafloor magnetic studies in the 1960s led to plate tectonics.
entries.changed: 1912: Wegener proposes drift; largely rejected. 1963: Vine & Matthews magnetic stripes. Late 1960s: plate tectonics becomes consensus.

media.title: The Plate Tectonics Revolution: Crash Course Geography #19

entries.title: Apollo 11 Moon landing
entries.mainstream: First crewed landing on the Moon, July 1969.

alternatives.label: Hoax claims
alternatives.text: Conspiracy claims that the landings were faked are rejected by overwhelming evidence (retroreflectors, samples, independent tracking).

entries.title: Gunung Padang "oldest pyramid" claim
entries.mainstream: A 2023 paper claimed parts of the Indonesian site were built over 20,000 years ago; the journal retracted it in 2024 because the dated soil was not shown to be connected to human activity.

alternatives.label: Proponents
alternatives.text: The authors and supporters maintain an ancient construction date.

entries.changed: 2023: published; 2024: retracted.

sources.title: RETRACTED: Geo‐archaeological prospecting of Gunung Padang buried prehistoric pyramid in West Java, Indonesia

entries.title: ʻOumuamua: first known interstellar object
entries.mainstream: Discovered in October 2017 by Pan-STARRS in Hawaii, ʻOumuamua was the first object confirmed to come from outside the Solar System; it was small, elongated and showed slight non-gravitational acceleration.

alternatives.label: Natural origin explanations
alternatives.text: Researchers have proposed outgassing of hydrogen or nitrogen ice, among other natural causes, for the acceleration.

alternatives.label: Artificial origin (minority view)
alternatives.text: Astronomer Avi Loeb suggested it could be an artificial light-sail; most astronomers consider a natural origin far more likely.

sources.title: A brief visit from a red and extremely elongated interstellar asteroid

entries.title: US House hearing on UAP (UFOs)
entries.mainstream: On 26 July 2023 a US House Oversight subcommittee held a hearing on unidentified anomalous phenomena. That the hearing and testimony happened is confirmed; claims made in it (e.g. of recovered non-human craft) are unverified and were denied by the US Department of Defense.

alternatives.label: Disclosure view
alternatives.text: Some witnesses and supporters argue the government holds evidence of non-human technology.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Officials and many scientists say no verifiable evidence of extraterrestrial technology has been presented.

sources.title: House Oversight Committee hearing page: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (26 July 2023)

entries.title: First image of a black hole (M87*)
entries.mainstream: In April 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration published the first image of a black hole’s shadow, in galaxy M87.

sources.title: First M87 Event Horizon Telescope Results. I. The Shadow of the Supermassive Black Hole

entries.title: Kenneth Arnold sighting ("flying saucers")
entries.mainstream: On 24 June 1947 pilot Kenneth Arnold reported nine fast objects near Mount Rainier; press coverage coined "flying saucer". The sighting is documented; what he saw is unexplained.

alternatives.label: Conventional explanations
alternatives.text: Proposed explanations include mirages, birds, or aircraft.

alternatives.label: Extraterrestrial craft
alternatives.text: Some UFO researchers regard it as an early sighting of non-human craft.

entries.title: Roswell incident
entries.mainstream: In July 1947 debris was recovered near Roswell, New Mexico; the US Air Force later (1994–97 reports) identified it as from Project Mogul, a classified balloon programme.

alternatives.label: Crashed alien craft
alternatives.text: Many UFO researchers and witnesses since the late 1970s claim an alien spacecraft and bodies were recovered and covered up.

entries.changed: 1947: Army announces a "flying disc", then a weather balloon. Late 1970s: interest revives with alien-crash claims. 1994–1997: USAF reports attribute debris to Project Mogul.

entries.title: Project Blue Book
entries.mainstream: US Air Force programme that investigated over 12,000 UFO reports; most were explained, a minority remained "unidentified". Closed in 1969 after the Condon Report.

alternatives.label: Cover-up view
alternatives.text: Some critics argue the project was designed to debunk rather than investigate.

sources.title: Project Blue Book – Unidentified Flying Objects (US National Archives)

entries.title: Betty and Barney Hill abduction claim
entries.mainstream: The Hills reported a UFO sighting in New Hampshire in September 1961 and later, under hypnosis, described an abduction — the first widely publicised abduction account.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Psychologists note hypnosis can create false memories and suggest cultural influences.

alternatives.label: Genuine abduction
alternatives.text: Supporters regard their account, including Betty Hill's "star map", as evidence of contact.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Barney and Betty Hill incident

entries.title: Ancient astronauts (Chariots of the Gods?)
entries.mainstream: Erich von Däniken's 1968 book popularised the claim that extraterrestrials visited ancient peoples and inspired monuments and religions. Archaeologists widely reject it as pseudoarchaeology.

alternatives.label: Ancient astronaut theory
alternatives.text: Proponents cite Nazca lines, pyramids and sacred texts as evidence of ancient contact.

alternatives.label: Criticism
alternatives.text: Critics note factual errors and argue it underestimates ancient peoples' abilities.

entries.title: Rendlesham Forest incident
entries.mainstream: In December 1980 US Air Force personnel near RAF Woodbridge, England, reported lights and a craft in Rendlesham Forest; Lt Col Halt's memo documents the reports.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Investigators suggest the Orford Ness lighthouse, a bright meteor and stars as explanations.

alternatives.label: UFO landing
alternatives.text: Some witnesses maintain they encountered a craft of unknown origin.

entries.title: Phoenix Lights
entries.mainstream: On 13 March 1997 thousands reported lights over Arizona. The later lights were attributed by the US military to flares dropped during an exercise; the earlier V-shaped formation is attributed by many to aircraft.

alternatives.label: Unexplained craft
alternatives.text: Some witnesses, including then-governor Fife Symington (later), describe a huge structured craft.

entries.title: USS Nimitz "Tic Tac" encounter
entries.mainstream: In November 2004 US Navy pilots from the Nimitz carrier group reported a fast white object; infrared video ("FLIR1") was released in 2017 and acknowledged by the Navy in 2020.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Analysts have proposed sensor artefacts or misidentified aircraft.

alternatives.label: Advanced unknown technology
alternatives.text: Some pilots and researchers say its performance exceeds known technology.

entries.title: Fermi paradox ("Where is everybody?")
entries.mainstream: In 1950 Enrico Fermi asked why, if intelligent life is common, there is no evidence of it. The question is real; proposed answers range from rarity of life to self-destruction to deliberate silence.

alternatives.label: Rare Earth
alternatives.text: Complex life may be very rare.

alternatives.label: Zoo / hidden contact
alternatives.text: Some propose aliens avoid contact or are already present (speculative).

entries.title: Wow! signal
entries.mainstream: A strong narrowband radio signal detected by Ohio State's Big Ear telescope on 15 August 1977; it was never detected again and its origin is unknown.

alternatives.label: Natural source
alternatives.text: Proposals include hydrogen-cloud emission or interference.

alternatives.label: Artificial origin
alternatives.text: Some consider it a possible extraterrestrial transmission.

media.author: Credit: Big Ear Radio Observatory and North American AstroPhysical Observatory (NAAPO).

entries.title: Oklo natural nuclear reactors
entries.mainstream: About 1.7–2 billion years ago, uranium deposits at Oklo, Gabon, sustained natural nuclear fission reactions; discovered by French scientists in 1972.

alternatives.label: Artificial reactor
alternatives.text: Occasionally cited in fringe literature as an ancient artificial reactor; geologists explain it fully by natural processes.

entries.changed: 1972: discovered from an anomalous uranium-235 deficit in ore.

entries.title: Nazca Lines
entries.mainstream: Large geoglyphs in southern Peru made by the Nazca culture c. 500 BCE–500 CE, thought to have ritual functions; UNESCO World Heritage Site.

alternatives.label: Alien runways
alternatives.text: Von Däniken suggested they were landing strips for visitors; archaeologists reject this.

sources.title: Lines and Geoglyphs of Nasca and Palpa (UNESCO)

entries.title: "Baghdad battery"
entries.mainstream: Clay jars with copper cylinders and iron rods from Parthian/Sasanian Mesopotamia; most archaeologists think they stored scrolls or similar, not electricity.

alternatives.label: Ancient electricity
alternatives.text: Some suggest they were galvanic cells used for electroplating or ritual effects.

entries.title: Voynich manuscript
entries.mainstream: An illustrated manuscript in an undeciphered script; its vellum was radiocarbon-dated to 1404–1438. Held at Yale's Beinecke Library.

alternatives.label: Hoax or glossolalia
alternatives.text: Some argue it is meaningless text.

alternatives.label: Cipher or lost language
alternatives.text: Many decipherment claims exist; none widely accepted.

entries.title: Dropa stones
entries.mainstream: Stories from the 1960s claimed stone discs from China recorded an alien crash 12,000 years ago; no verifiable discs, scholars or excavation records have been found.

alternatives.label: Believers
alternatives.text: Some ancient-astronaut writers still cite them.

entries.title: Piri Reis map
entries.mainstream: An Ottoman world map of 1513 by Piri Reis, compiled from earlier sources including a Columbus map.

alternatives.label: Ice-free Antarctica
alternatives.text: Charles Hapgood and later authors claimed it shows Antarctica's coast without ice; historians attribute the coastline to distorted South America.

entries.title: Fast radio bursts discovered
entries.mainstream: Millisecond radio flashes from distant galaxies, first reported in 2007; many are now linked to magnetars.

alternatives.label: Technosignatures
alternatives.text: A few researchers have speculated about artificial origins; this is not mainstream.

sources.title: A Bright Millisecond Radio Burst of Extragalactic Origin

entries.title: Tabby's Star dimming
entries.mainstream: Star KIC 8462852 showed unusual irregular dimming (reported 2015). Follow-up observations favour dust as the cause.

alternatives.label: Megastructure
alternatives.text: Early media speculation about an alien megastructure; follow-up work disfavours it.

entries.title: Crop circles
entries.mainstream: Doug Bower and Dave Chorley admitted in 1991 to making many English crop circles from 1976; most circles are attributed to people.

alternatives.label: Paranormal origin
alternatives.text: Some still attribute certain formations to unknown energies or UFOs.

entries.changed: 1991: Bower and Chorley demonstrate their methods.

entries.title: Cottingley Fairies
entries.mainstream: Photographs taken by two girls in 1917 appeared to show fairies; endorsed by Arthur Conan Doyle, they were admitted in 1983 to be faked with paper cut-outs.

entries.title: Silurian hypothesis (pre-human industry?)
entries.mainstream: Gavin Schmidt and Adam Frank (2018) asked whether an industrial civilisation millions of years ago would be detectable in the geological record; the authors do not claim one existed.

alternatives.label: Speculative use
alternatives.text: Some popular writers cite it as support for lost pre-human civilisations, which the authors do not argue.

sources.title: The Silurian hypothesis: would it be possible to detect an industrial civilization in the geological record?

entries.title: Sumerian King List
entries.dateNote: Earliest copies c. 2100–1800 BCE
entries.mainstream: A Mesopotamian text listing kings "before" and "after the flood", with pre-flood reigns of tens of thousands of years. Scholars treat early parts as legendary.

alternatives.label: Literal reading
alternatives.text: Some alternative authors read the long reigns literally or as records of non-human rulers.

sources.title: The Sumerian king list: translation (ETCSL, University of Oxford)

entries.title: Puma Punku (Tiwanaku)
entries.mainstream: Part of the Tiwanaku site in Bolivia (c. 500–1000 CE), known for precisely cut andesite and sandstone blocks.

alternatives.label: Ancient-astronaut readings
alternatives.text: Some claim the precision implies lost or alien technology; archaeologists attribute it to Tiwanaku stoneworking.

sources.title: Tiwanaku: Spiritual and Political Centre of the Tiwanaku Culture (UNESCO)

entries.title: Baalbek megaliths
entries.mainstream: Roman temple complex in Lebanon with some of the largest cut stones ever moved (the Trilithon, ~800 t); dated to the Roman period.

alternatives.label: Older/lost civilisation
alternatives.text: Some authors claim the foundation stones are much older or required lost technology.

entries.title: "Bosnian pyramids" claim
entries.mainstream: In 2005 Semir Osmanagić claimed hills near Visoko, Bosnia, were ancient pyramids; geologists identify them as natural formations (flatirons).

alternatives.label: Proponents
alternatives.text: Supporters continue excavations and maintain an artificial origin.

entries.title: Nebra sky disc
entries.mainstream: A Bronze Age bronze disc with gold sky symbols found in Germany in 1999; once doubted as a fake, now widely accepted as authentic.

alternatives.label: Dating debate
alternatives.text: Some researchers have argued for an Iron Age date.

sources.title: Archaeometallurgical investigation of the Nebra Sky Disc

entries.title: Kensington Runestone
entries.mainstream: A stone with runic inscription claiming a 1362 Norse visit, found in Minnesota in 1898; most runologists regard it as a 19th-century creation.

alternatives.label: Authentic
alternatives.text: Some researchers and local supporters argue it is genuine.

entries.title: Indus Valley Civilisation
entries.mainstream: Bronze Age urban civilisation (mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE) in present-day Pakistan and India, with planned cities such as Mohenjo-daro; its script is undeciphered.

entries.title: Romulus and the founding of Rome
entries.mainstream: Roman tradition dates the city's founding by Romulus to 753 BCE; archaeology shows settlement on the Palatine from earlier.

entries.title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
entries.mainstream: The last western emperor was deposed in 476 CE; historians debate whether it was a "fall" or gradual transformation.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

entries.title: Mount Mazama eruption & Klamath legend
entries.mainstream: Mount Mazama in Oregon erupted ~7,700 years ago forming Crater Lake. Klamath oral tradition describes a battle between Llao and Skell that some scholars link to the eruption.

alternatives.label: Caution
alternatives.text: Others note the difficulty of linking oral traditions to specific events.

entries.title: Wegener proposes continental drift
entries.mainstream: Alfred Wegener presented continental drift in 1912; widely rejected for decades, it was vindicated by plate tectonics in the 1960s.

entries.title: Anunnaki: scholarship vs ancient-astronaut claims
entries.mainstream: The Anunnaki are a group of deities in Mesopotamian texts. Assyriologists read them as gods within Sumerian/Akkadian religion.

alternatives.label: Sitchin's claims
alternatives.text: Zecharia Sitchin (1976) claimed they were extraterrestrials from a planet "Nibiru" who created humans; Assyriologists reject his translations.

entries.title: Vimanas (flying chariots in Indian texts)
entries.mainstream: Flying palaces or chariots of gods appear in Sanskrit epics such as the Ramayana (e.g. the Pushpaka vimana).

alternatives.label: Ancient aircraft
alternatives.text: Some claim they describe real ancient aircraft; the 20th-century "Vaimanika Shastra" text cited for this was shown by a 1974 IISc study to be aeronautically unworkable.

entries.title: Dogon and Sirius B
entries.mainstream: Griaule and Dieterlen reported (1950s) that the Dogon of Mali knew of Sirius's invisible companion. Anthropologist Walter van Beek's 1991 restudy found no such knowledge among the Dogon.

alternatives.label: Ancient contact
alternatives.text: Robert Temple's "The Sirius Mystery" (1976) argued it came from extraterrestrials.

alternatives.label: Cultural contamination
alternatives.text: Others suggest Western astronomy reached the Dogon before Griaule's work.

sources.title: Dogon Restudied: A Field Evaluation of the Work of Marcel Griaule

entries.title: Nephilim (Genesis 6)
entries.mainstream: Genesis 6:1–4 mentions "sons of God" and the Nephilim; 1 Enoch expands this into the Watchers story. Interpretations vary between fallen angels, human lineages and giants.

alternatives.label: Ancient-astronaut reading
alternatives.text: Some modern writers interpret them as extraterrestrial or hybrid beings (speculative).

entries.title: Ezekiel's vision of the wheels
entries.mainstream: The prophet Ezekiel describes a vision of living creatures and wheels (Ezekiel 1); traditionally interpreted theologically.

alternatives.label: Spacecraft interpretation
alternatives.text: NASA engineer Josef Blumrich's 1974 book argued it described a spacecraft; biblical scholars reject this.

entries.title: Miracle of the Sun (Fátima)
entries.mainstream: On 13 October 1917 a crowd at Fátima, Portugal, reported the sun dancing; the Catholic Church approved it as worthy of belief.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Scientists suggest optical effects from staring at the sun, or mass suggestion.

alternatives.label: UFO reading
alternatives.text: Some UFO writers interpret it as a sighting.

entries.title: Loch Ness Monster and the "surgeon's photograph"
entries.mainstream: The famous 1934 photograph was revealed in 1994 to be a hoax using a toy submarine; a 2018 eDNA survey found no reptile DNA in the loch.

alternatives.label: Believers
alternatives.text: Sightings continue and some believe an unknown animal lives there.

entries.title: Patterson–Gimlin Bigfoot film
entries.mainstream: A 1967 film shows a large ape-like figure in California; scientists generally consider it a person in a costume, though no costume has been conclusively produced.

alternatives.label: Genuine creature
alternatives.text: Some researchers argue the gait and proportions are not human.

entries.title: Great Zimbabwe
entries.mainstream: Stone city in present-day Zimbabwe built by ancestors of the Shona, c. 11th–15th centuries CE; a major inland trading centre linked to the Indian Ocean. UNESCO World Heritage Site.

alternatives.label: Non-African builders (colonial claim)
alternatives.text: Colonial-era writers often denied African authorship and attributed the ruins to outsiders; archaeology has established local Shona construction.

entries.changed: Colonial period: African origin denied. Mid–late 20th century: archaeology confirms local construction.

entries.title: Mapungubwe kingdom
entries.mainstream: First major indigenous kingdom in southern Africa (c. 900–1300 CE) at the Limpopo–Shashe confluence; gold artefacts and trade goods show Indian Ocean links. Power later shifted toward Great Zimbabwe.

media.title: Mapungubwe - Lost Kingdoms of Africa - Great Zimbabwe - BBC 4

entries.title: Kingdom of Aksum
entries.mainstream: Powerful Horn of Africa state (c. 1st–8th centuries CE) controlling Red Sea trade; known for monumental stelae, coinage and early adoption of Christianity.

media.title: The Rise Of Aksum - History Of Africa With Zeinab Badawi [Episode 5]

entries.title: Nok culture terracotta
entries.mainstream: Iron Age culture of central Nigeria (roughly 9th century BCE–early CE) known for distinctive terracotta figures; among the earliest iron-working societies in West Africa.

entries.title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage
entries.mainstream: Mansa Musa of Mali made the hajj in 1324–25; contemporary Arabic sources describe his wealth and gold gifts in Cairo. The Mali Empire was a major West African state.

media.title: Mansa Musa, one of the wealthiest people who ever lived - Jessica Smith

entries.title: Benin Bronzes
entries.mainstream: Brass and bronze plaques and sculptures from the Kingdom of Benin (present-day Nigeria), produced from at least the 13th century; many were looted by British forces in 1897 and are now in museums worldwide.

media.title: George the Poet – The Benin bronze

entries.title: Blombos Cave symbolic behaviour
entries.dateNote: Key assemblages c. 100–70 ka
entries.mainstream: Blombos Cave (South Africa) yields engraved ochre, shell beads and tool kits dated to roughly 100–70 thousand years ago — early evidence of symbolic behaviour in Homo sapiens.

entries.title: Border Cave early modern humans
entries.mainstream: Border Cave (South Africa–Eswatini border) has Middle Stone Age deposits with early modern human remains and material culture spanning roughly 200–40 thousand years ago.

entries.title: Meroë and the Nubian pyramids
entries.mainstream: Capital of the Kingdom of Kush in present-day Sudan; hundreds of steep Nubian pyramids mark royal burials from about the 8th century BCE to the 4th century CE.

sources.title: Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe (UNESCO)

media.title: Amazing Drone Footage of Nubian Pyramids | Expedition Raw

entries.title: Laetoli footprints
entries.mainstream: Fossilised bipedal footprints at Laetoli, Tanzania, dated to about 3.66 million years ago and attributed to early hominins (often Australopithecus afarensis).

entries.title: Jōmon pottery
entries.mainstream: Early pottery of Japan's Jōmon period; some vessels date to about 14,000 BCE or earlier — among the world's oldest known ceramics.

entries.title: Sanxingdui
entries.mainstream: Bronze Age site in Sichuan, China, with large bronze masks, trees and statues unlike typical Central Plains styles; flourished roughly late 2nd–early 1st millennium BCE.

alternatives.label: Lost / unknown civilisation
alternatives.text: Popular accounts emphasise mystery; archaeologists link it to the ancient Shu culture.

alternatives.label: Alien contact (speculative)
alternatives.text: Fringe writers occasionally cite the masks as non-human; this is not supported by archaeology.

entries.title: Xia dynasty debate
entries.dateNote: Traditional dates c. 2070–1600 BCE
entries.mainstream: Traditional Chinese historiography places a Xia dynasty before the Shang (c. 2070–1600 BCE). The Erlitou culture is often proposed as Xia, but the link remains debated.

alternatives.label: Legendary only
alternatives.text: Some scholars treat early Xia kings as legendary until firmer textual–archaeological links emerge.

alternatives.label: Confirmed dynasty
alternatives.text: Others argue Erlitou and related sites substantiate the Xia.

entries.title: Indus (Harappan) script
entries.mainstream: Short inscriptions from the Indus Valley Civilisation remain undeciphered; whether the signs encode language is still debated.

alternatives.label: Non-linguistic symbols
alternatives.text: Some researchers argue the signs were non-linguistic markers.

alternatives.label: Undeciphered language
alternatives.text: Others treat them as writing awaiting decipherment.

entries.title: Angkor
entries.mainstream: Capital region of the Khmer Empire in present-day Cambodia (c. 9th–15th centuries), including Angkor Wat; one of the largest pre-industrial urban complexes.

media.title: 5. The Khmer Empire - Fall of the God Kings

entries.title: Nan Madol
entries.mainstream: Megalithic basalt city built on artificial islets off Pohnpei, Micronesia; associated with the Saudeleur dynasty. Construction peaked around the 12th–13th centuries CE.

alternatives.label: Lost advanced civilisation
alternatives.text: Some alternative writers claim unknown builders or lost technology; archaeology attributes it to local Micronesian societies.

sources.title: Nan Madol: Ceremonial Centre of Eastern Micronesia (UNESCO)

media.title: Ancient City of Nan Madol | Lost Cities With Albert Lin

entries.title: Rapa Nui (Easter Island) moai
entries.mainstream: Nearly 1,000 stone statues carved by Polynesian settlers on Rapa Nui, mainly c. 13th–16th centuries. Ecological and social causes of later societal stress remain researched.

alternatives.label: Alien / lost civilisation builders
alternatives.text: Fringe theories deny Polynesian capability; archaeology and genetics support Polynesian settlement and craftsmanship.

media.title: The Mysteries of the Moai on Easter Island | National Geographic

entries.title: Lapita culture
entries.mainstream: Austronesian seafaring culture of Remote Oceania (c. 1500–500 BCE) marked by dentate-stamped pottery; ancestral to many Polynesian, Micronesian and some Melanesian societies.

entries.title: Wandjina rock art
entries.dateNote: Tradition ongoing; some paintings may be thousands of years old
entries.mainstream: Wandjina are ancestral creator beings in the rock art and oral traditions of Kimberley Aboriginal peoples (north-western Australia). Paintings are maintained by Traditional Owners.

alternatives.label: Ancient astronaut reading
alternatives.text: Some popular writers misread the halo-like headdresses as spacesuits; Aboriginal custodians and archaeologists reject this.

entries.title: Kupe and Māori discovery traditions
entries.dateNote: Settlement archaeology c. late 1200s CE; traditions vary by iwi
entries.mainstream: Māori oral traditions name ancestors such as Kupe among early Polynesian voyagers to Aotearoa/New Zealand. Archaeology places Polynesian settlement around the late 13th century CE.

entries.title: Cahokia
entries.mainstream: Largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico, near present-day St. Louis; peaked c. 1050–1200 CE with massive earthen mounds including Monks Mound.

entries.title: Teotihuacan
entries.mainstream: Major Mesoamerican city in the Valley of Mexico (flourished c. 1st–6th centuries CE) with the Pyramid of the Sun and Avenue of the Dead; its rulers' ethnic identity remains debated.

entries.title: Olmec colossal heads
entries.mainstream: Large basalt portrait heads of the Olmec civilisation (Gulf Coast Mexico, roughly 1200–400 BCE); transported from distant quarries without wheeled vehicles.

alternatives.label: African contact claim
alternatives.text: Ivan Van Sertima and others argued Negroid features imply ancient African contact; most Mesoamericanists reject this as unsupported.

alternatives.label: Alien / lost technology
alternatives.text: Fringe accounts cite the size as evidence of unknown tech; archaeologists attribute them to Olmec labour organisation.

media.title: The little-known 'mother culture' that inspired the Maya - BBC REEL

entries.title: Caral-Supe
entries.mainstream: Early urban centre in Peru's Supe Valley (c. 2600–2000 BCE), among the oldest known cities in the Americas; monumental platform mounds without ceramics in early phases.

entries.title: Monte Verde
entries.mainstream: Late Pleistocene site in southern Chile with accepted dates around 14,500 years ago (and debated older claims), important evidence against a strict "Clovis First" peopling model.
entries.changed: 1997 onward: a research consensus panel accepted the c. 14.5 ka occupation, shifting the peopling debate.

entries.title: Clovis First debate
entries.mainstream: Clovis culture (c. 13,000 years ago) was long held to be the first widespread people in the Americas. Pre-Clovis sites such as Monte Verde challenged that model; the debate continues on timing and routes.

alternatives.label: Still Clovis-centred views
alternatives.text: Some researchers still emphasise Clovis as the first pan-continental culture while accepting limited earlier coastal presence.

entries.changed: Late 20th–21st century: pre-Clovis sites gained wider acceptance.

entries.title: Ica stones
entries.mainstream: Carved andesite stones from Ica, Peru, popularised in the 1960s depicting dinosaurs and advanced technology. Farmers admitted carving them for collectors; no secure archaeological context.

alternatives.label: Believers
alternatives.text: Some ancient-astronaut and creationist writers still treat them as genuine ancient artefacts.

entries.title: Acámbaro figures
entries.mainstream: Thousands of ceramic figurines including dinosaur-like creatures collected near Acámbaro, Mexico, from 1944. Mainstream archaeology regards them as modern fakes made for Waldemar Julsrud.

alternatives.label: Genuine ancient artefacts
alternatives.text: A minority of fringe researchers claim thermoluminescence or context supports antiquity; this is not accepted by mainstream archaeology.

entries.title: Quetzalcoatl
entries.mainstream: Feathered-serpent deity of Mesoamerica, important in Teotihuacan, Toltec and Aztec religion; associated with wind, learning and priesthood.

alternatives.label: Bearded foreign god / alien reading
alternatives.text: Colonial and later writers sometimes equated Quetzalcoatl with a historical foreigner or visitor; these readings are speculative.

entries.title: Viracocha
entries.mainstream: Creator deity in Andean (Inca and earlier) tradition, sometimes described as a bearded culture-bringer who walked away across the sea.

alternatives.label: Ancient visitor claim
alternatives.text: Some 19th–20th century and fringe authors read Viracocha as a memory of overseas or extraterrestrial visitors (speculative).

entries.title: Westall UFO encounter (1966)
entries.mainstream: On 6 April 1966 hundreds of students and staff at Westall High School (Melbourne, Australia) reported a low-flying silver disc that landed in a nearby field then rose and departed. Official explanations proposed a balloon or aircraft; many witnesses disagree.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Proposed prosaic causes include weather balloons or light aircraft.

alternatives.label: Unknown craft
alternatives.text: Witnesses and some researchers maintain an unexplained craft was seen.

entries.title: Ariel School UFO encounter (Ruwa, 1994)
entries.mainstream: On 16 September 1994 about 60 children at Ariel School near Ruwa, Zimbabwe, reported a landed craft and beings. Harvard psychiatrist John Mack interviewed pupils; explanations proposed include mass hysteria, a known meteor fireball that day, or a hoax.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Critics cite contagion, expectation and a bright fireball reported over southern Africa that morning.

alternatives.label: Contact experience
alternatives.text: Mack and some witnesses treated the children's accounts as genuine encounters.

entries.title: Vela Incident
entries.mainstream: On 22 September 1979 a US Vela satellite detected a double flash over the southern Atlantic/Indian Ocean consistent with a nuclear test. The US government never confirmed a test; suspected parties include South Africa and/or Israel.

alternatives.label: Nuclear test
alternatives.text: Many analysts conclude a clandestine test occurred.

alternatives.label: Non-nuclear explanation
alternatives.text: A 1980 scientific panel favoured a meteoroid striking the satellite; that view remains contested.

entries.title: Mokele-mbembe
entries.mainstream: Central African folklore describes a large water creature in the Congo Basin, popularised in the West as a possible living sauropod. No specimen or convincing evidence has been produced; biologists treat it as legend or misidentified animals.

alternatives.label: Living dinosaur (cryptozoology)
alternatives.text: Some cryptozoologists treat expedition anecdotes as evidence of a surviving dinosaur (speculative).

entries.title: Popobawa
entries.mainstream: Popobawa is a shape-shifting spirit in Zanzibar folklore, associated with panic waves (notably 1995) in which people reported nocturnal attacks. Anthropologists study it as a social and psychological phenomenon.

entries.title: Nyaminyami (Zambezi river spirit)
entries.dateNote: Tradition older; dam-era events 1950s–60s
entries.mainstream: Nyaminyami is the Zambezi River god/serpent in Tonga tradition. Floods during Kariba Dam construction (1950s–60s) were widely linked by local people to the spirit's anger at separation from his wife.

entries.title: Wilusa and the historicity of Troy
entries.dateNote: Alaksandu treaty c. 1280 BCE; Homeric tradition later
entries.mainstream: Hittite texts mention Wilusa and a conflict involving Alaksandu — widely identified with Ilios/Troy and Alexandros (Paris). Combined with Schliemann's and later excavations, this supports a historical core behind the Trojan War tradition.
entries.changed: Late 20th century: Hittite geography and the Alaksandu treaty strengthened the Troy–Wilusa link.

entries.title: Izanagi and Izanami
entries.dateNote: Recorded in 8th-century chronicles; mythic time
entries.mainstream: Creator pair in Japanese mythology (Kojiki and Nihon Shoki) who stir the ocean to form the first islands and produce deities; Izanami dies after birthing the fire god.

entries.title: Bunjil
entries.dateNote: Living oral tradition; date is schematic for timeline placement
entries.mainstream: Bunjil (or Bunjil the Eaglehawk) is a creator ancestor in Kulin Nation traditions of south-eastern Australia, associated with the creation of people, animals and landscape laws.

entries.title: Curuçá (Brazilian Tunguska) event
entries.mainstream: In August 1930 a bright fireball and explosions were reported near the Curuçá River in Brazil's Amazon. Later researchers compared it to Tunguska; documentation is thinner and the event remains poorly constrained.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Accounts may mix a meteor airburst with exaggeration or other phenomena.

alternatives.label: Major airburst
alternatives.text: Some atmospheric scientists treat it as a significant Tunguska-like airburst.

entries.title: Rock-hewn churches of Lalibela
entries.dateNote: Traditional date = reign of King Lalibela (c. 1181–1221); some parts may be older
entries.mainstream: Eleven monolithic churches carved down into the rock in the Ethiopian Highlands, traditionally attributed to the Zagwe king Gebre Meskel Lalibela (r. c. 1181–1221) as a "New Jerusalem". Many archaeologists think they took shape over several construction phases. UNESCO World Heritage Site (1978) and still an active pilgrimage centre.

alternatives.label: Built with angelic help (tradition)
alternatives.text: Local tradition, recorded by 16th-century Portuguese visitors, attributes the churches to angels working alongside human builders; this is a religious tradition, not a testable claim.

alternatives.label: Older Aksumite origin
alternatives.text: Archaeologist David Phillipson proposed that some structures were first cut c. 600–800 CE as fortifications or palaces and only later converted to churches; others dispute this dating.

entries.title: Kilwa Kisiwani and the Swahili coast
entries.mainstream: Island city off southern Tanzania that led the Kilwa Sultanate, a Swahili trading state whose influence peaked in the 13th–15th centuries. Kilwa minted its own coins (found as far inland as Great Zimbabwe); Ibn Battuta praised it c. 1331; the Portuguese sacked it in 1505. UNESCO World Heritage Site.

alternatives.label: Founding tradition
alternatives.text: The Kilwa Chronicle tells of a founding by a Persian (Shirazi) prince; historians debate how far this reflects actual migration versus later prestige claims, noting little evidence of Shirazi Shia Islam on the coast.

sources.title: Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara (UNESCO)

entries.title: Timbuktu manuscripts
entries.dateNote: Manuscripts date from the late 13th to the early 20th century; rescue 2012–13
entries.mainstream: A vast, still uncounted body of manuscripts (late 13th to early 20th centuries; one project alone has photographed over 150,000) on law, religion, astronomy, medicine, history and more, kept for generations in Timbuktu family libraries in Mali. In 2012–13, during the Northern Mali conflict, 4,203 were burned or stolen, while families and librarians smuggled most of the rest to Bamako; large digitisation projects followed.

alternatives.label: Hidden knowledge angle
alternatives.text: Because most manuscripts remain uncatalogued and unstudied, their full content is unknown; claims about what they might reveal are speculative until they are read and published.

media.title: Preserving the priceless manuscripts of Timbuktu

entries.title: Ishango bone
entries.dateNote: Usually dated c. 20,000 years ago; dating debated
entries.mainstream: Engraved bone tool (animal species undetermined) found in 1950 at Ishango, DR Congo, by Jean de Heinzelin; now usually dated to about 20,000 years ago. Its grouped notches are often described as one of the oldest possible mathematical artefacts; older notched bones exist, such as the c. 42,000-year-old Lebombo bone from southern Africa.

alternatives.label: Arithmetic / prime numbers
alternatives.text: De Heinzelin and later writers suggested the notch groups show deliberate arithmetic, and one column has been read as the primes between 10 and 20 (speculative; may be coincidence).

alternatives.label: Lunar calendar
alternatives.text: Some researchers have proposed the marks track lunar phases (speculative).

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: The marks could be tallies or simply grip-improving scratches; dating is also debated because volcanic activity disturbed carbon ratios.

entries.title: Prester John: the lost Christian king
entries.mainstream: Medieval European legend of a rich Christian priest-king ruling a lost realm "in the Indies". It is first recorded by Otto of Freising (1145), and a widely copied Letter of Prester John (c. 1165, probably a Western forgery) spread it. The legend was attached first to Central Asia and later to Ethiopia, whose rulers never used the title.

alternatives.label: Real kernel
alternatives.text: Scholars link the legend to real but distant Christians (Church of the East converts such as the Kerait of Central Asia, Christian Ethiopia), and the 1145 report to the Qara Khitai victory over the Seljuks at Qatwan in 1141.

alternatives.label: Propaganda
alternatives.text: Some historians read it partly as crusade-era wishful thinking or propaganda about a powerful eastern ally.

entries.changed: 12th c.: placed in Asia. c. 1250 onward: increasingly identified with Ethiopia. 17th c.: Hiob Ludolf shows no native Ethiopian link and the search fades.

entries.title: Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang (mercury rivers)
entries.mainstream: Tomb complex of China's first emperor near Xi'an, built 246–208 BCE under a 76 m mound and guarded by the Terracotta Army. The main tomb chamber has never been opened. Sima Qian wrote that it contained rivers and seas of mercury; soil surveys over the mound have measured anomalously high mercury levels.

alternatives.label: Sima Qian confirmed
alternatives.text: Many researchers see the soil mercury as support for Sima Qian's account of mercury rivers in the sealed chamber.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Some argue the mercury readings may reflect local industrial pollution; only excavation could settle it, and archaeologists have delayed opening the tomb over preservation and safety concerns.

sources.title: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor (UNESCO)
Wikipedia: Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang

media.title: The First Emperor's Mega Tomb: Uncovering a Lost World | SPECIAL | National Geographic

entries.title: Borobudur
entries.mainstream: Huge 9th-century Mahayana Buddhist monument in Central Java, Indonesia, built as a stepped stupa with thousands of relief panels. It was later abandoned, possibly after volcanic eruptions and the shift of power to East Java (10th century) or after conversion to Islam, and lay under ash and jungle. Restored with UNESCO by 1983; World Heritage Site 1991.

alternatives.label: Abandonment mystery
alternatives.text: Why and when Borobudur was abandoned is still unresolved; volcanic, political and religious explanations are all proposed.

entries.changed: 1814: brought to European attention by Stamford Raffles after local Javanese reported it. 1975–82: major Indonesian–UNESCO restoration.

entries.title: Zheng He's treasure voyages
entries.mainstream: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming admiral Zheng He commanded seven large fleets across Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean as far as Arabia and East Africa (a giraffe from Malindi was presented at court as a qilin). The voyages ended and Ming China turned inward.

alternatives.label: China discovered America (1421 claim)
alternatives.text: Gavin Menzies's 2002 book 1421 argued that Zheng He's fleets reached the Americas and circled the globe; historians reject this as pseudohistory for lack of evidence.

entries.title: Homo floresiensis ("hobbits") and the Ebu Gogo
entries.mainstream: A small-bodied archaic human species found in 2003 at Liang Bua cave on Flores, Indonesia. Revised dating (2016) puts the skeletal remains at about 100,000–60,000 years ago and stone tools to about 50,000 years ago, around when modern humans arrived. Its small size is usually explained by island dwarfism.

alternatives.label: Pathology hypothesis
alternatives.text: Some researchers argued the LB1 skeleton was a modern human with microcephaly or another disorder; later analyses mostly support a separate species.

alternatives.label: Folk memory (Ebu Gogo)
alternatives.text: Flores folklore tells of small, hairy "Ebu Gogo" people; ethnologist Gregory Forth suggested such tales might preserve memories of real hominins. This has little support since the remains were dated to well before recent times (speculative).

entries.changed: 2004: initially thought to have survived until c. 12,000 years ago, fuelling Ebu Gogo speculation. 2016: re-dating pushes the remains back to 100–60 ka.

entries.title: Siberian Ice Maiden (Ukok princess)
entries.mainstream: Naturally frozen mummy of a young woman of the Pazyryk culture (5th century BCE), found in 1993 by Natalia Polosmak on the Ukok Plateau in the Altai Republic, Siberia, with intact clothing, deer-style tattoos and sacrificed horses. Returned to Gorno-Altaisk in 2012.

alternatives.label: Indigenous view
alternatives.text: Many Altaians regard her as an ancestral figure (linked to the epic heroine Ochy-bala) and some have sought her reburial; further excavation on Ukok is barred at their request.

alternatives.label: Contested ancestry
alternatives.text: Genetic claims about her European or Altaian ancestry became politically charged; scholars caution against using them to settle modern identity disputes.

entries.title: Chaco Canyon and the Sun Dagger
entries.mainstream: Between about 900 and 1150 CE Chaco Canyon (New Mexico) was a major Ancestral Puebloan centre with great houses built from quarried sandstone and timber hauled long distances, linked by roads. On Fajada Butte, a "Sun Dagger" petroglyph where light passes through stone slabs onto spirals was recorded in 1977. UNESCO World Heritage Site.

alternatives.label: Deliberate solar–lunar calendar
alternatives.text: Researchers led by Anna Sofaer argue the Sun Dagger and building alignments track solstices, equinoxes and lunar cycles.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Others think some alignments may be coincidental; the extent of planned astronomy is debated. In 1989 erosion from visitors shifted one slab, reducing the site's precision.

entries.title: Kennewick Man (the Ancient One)
entries.dateNote: Lived c. 8,400–8,700 years ago; found 1996
entries.mainstream: Skeleton found in 1996 by the Columbia River in Washington State, radiocarbon-dated to about 8,400–8,700 years ago. A 2015 genome study found him closest to modern Native Americans. After nearly 20 years of legal dispute he was reburied by Columbia Basin tribes in 2017.

alternatives.label: Early non-Native origin (superseded)
alternatives.text: Early skull-shape analyses called him "Caucasoid", fuelling claims that ancient Europeans or Ainu-like people reached America first; ancient DNA did not support this.

entries.changed: 1996–2014: skull morphology suggests non-Native affinities. 2015: genome shows Native American ancestry. 2017: reburial.

sources.title: The ancestry and affiliations of Kennewick Man

entries.title: Polynesian–American contact (Kon-Tiki to genomes)
entries.mainstream: In 1947 Thor Heyerdahl's Kon-Tiki raft sailed from Peru to Polynesia to argue that South Americans settled Polynesia. Most scholars rejected that model, since language and archaeology show Polynesians came from the west. A 2020 genome study found Native American ancestry in eastern Polynesians from a single contact around 1200 CE, and the sweet potato's spread also points to pre-Columbian contact.

alternatives.label: Who travelled?
alternatives.text: It is unresolved whether Polynesian voyagers reached South America and returned, or South Americans drifted west; the genetic signal fits either (open question).

alternatives.label: Heyerdahl vindicated?
alternatives.text: Some see the genetics as partly vindicating Heyerdahl; most researchers note it shows brief contact, not South American settlement of Polynesia.

entries.changed: 1947: Kon-Tiki popularises an American-origin theory. Late 20th c.: rejected in favour of a western origin. 2020: genomics confirms limited contact c. 1200 CE.

sources.title: Native American gene flow into Polynesia predating Easter Island settlement

entries.title: 1700 Cascadia earthquake and the "orphan tsunami"
entries.mainstream: On 26 January 1700 a magnitude ~8.7–9.2 megathrust earthquake ruptured about 1,000 km of the Cascadia subduction zone off western North America. Its tsunami reached Japan, where records of a wave with no felt earthquake allowed scientists in 1996 to date it to about 9 pm local time. Indigenous oral traditions from British Columbia to California describe a great quake and flood, e.g. the Huu-ay-aht account of Pachena Bay on a winter night.

alternatives.label: Thunderbird and Whale
alternatives.text: A widespread Northwest Coast motif of a battle between Thunderbird and Whale has been interpreted by some researchers as a mythic memory of earthquakes (interpretive).

entries.changed: Before 1980s: Cascadia not thought capable of giant quakes. 1980s–90s: "ghost forests" (tree rings ending 1699) and Japanese records confirm the 1700 event and oral histories.

entries.title: SN 1054: the Crab supernova "guest star"
entries.mainstream: Chinese astronomers recorded a "guest star" in July 1054 that remained visible until April 1056. Its remnant is the Crab Nebula, identified in the 20th century through the work of Lundmark, Mayall and Oort. The event is also mentioned in a later Japanese document and an Islamic-world source.

alternatives.label: Ancestral Puebloan record
alternatives.text: A pictograph near Peñasco Blanco in Chaco Canyon showing a star, crescent and hand is proposed to depict the supernova (plausible but unproven).

alternatives.label: Cahokia link
alternatives.text: Some have speculated that the event influenced the rise or building at Cahokia (speculative).

entries.title: Giant impact forms the Moon (Theia)
entries.mainstream: The leading explanation for the Moon's origin: about 4.5 billion years ago, 20–100 million years after the Solar System formed, a Mars-sized body (often called Theia) collided with the proto-Earth, and the debris re-accreted as the Moon. Proposed in 1946 (Daly) and revived in 1974–75 (Hartmann and Davis), it was tested against Apollo-sample data and computer simulations.

alternatives.label: Isotope puzzle
alternatives.text: Lunar and Earth rocks are almost identical isotopically, which some models struggle to explain; alternatives include a high-energy impact, a synestia, or multiple smaller impacts.

alternatives.label: Other models
alternatives.text: Older ideas such as capture or fission are now largely out of favour.

entries.changed: 1946: Daly proposes it. 1974–75: revived (Hartmann & Davis); Apollo-era data debated. 2001: high-resolution simulations (Canup & Asphaug).

entries.title: The Great Dying (end-Permian extinction)
entries.mainstream: The most severe mass extinction known, about 251.9 million years ago: roughly 81% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrate species vanished. High-precision dating (2014) puts the main pulse at about 60,000 years. The consensus cause is Siberian Traps flood-basalt eruptions, which drove warming, ocean acidification and oxygen-starved seas.

alternatives.label: Impact contribution
alternatives.text: Some researchers have proposed an asteroid impact played a role, but no accepted crater or impact signature has been confirmed (minority view).

entries.title: Draupner wave: sailors' "freak waves" proven
entries.mainstream: On 1 January 1995, a laser sensor on the Draupner gas platform in the North Sea measured a single 25.6 m wave, far larger than its surroundings. It was the first instrumental record of a rogue wave. For a long time sailors' reports of such waves had been treated as exaggeration because standard models made them vanishingly rare.
entries.changed: Before 1995: rogue waves widely regarded as sailors' tales. 1995: first measured. 2000s: satellite surveys show they are more common than models predicted.

entries.title: Budj Bim: eruption memory and eel traps
entries.dateNote: Eruption c. 36,900 years ago (Ar–Ar, 2020); eel traps from c. 6,600 years ago
entries.mainstream: Budj Bim (Mount Eccles), a volcano in south-western Victoria, Australia, was dated in 2020 by argon–argon methods to about 36,900 years ago. Gunditjmara creation stories tell of an ancestral being transforming into the volcano. The lava flow later hosted Gunditjmara eel-trap aquaculture, with one trap system carbon-dated to about 6,600 years ago (UNESCO World Heritage, 2019).

alternatives.label: Oldest oral tradition?
alternatives.text: Some researchers suggest Gunditjmara stories may preserve memory of eruptions in this volcanic province, possibly among the oldest surviving oral traditions; this is hard to test directly.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Others caution that stories could describe later eruptions in the region, or be later interpretations of the volcanic landscape.

sources.title: Early human occupation of southeastern Australia: New insights from 40Ar/39Ar dating of young volcanoes

entries.title: Volcanic winter of 536 ("worst year to be alive")
entries.mainstream: From 536 CE, at least three volcanic eruptions of uncertain location loaded the atmosphere with sulfate aerosols. Procopius wrote that the sun gave light "without brightness"; Northern Hemisphere summers cooled by up to ~2.5 °C, crops failed, and the Late Antique Little Ice Age (536–660) followed alongside the Plague of Justinian. Ice-core and tree-ring work published in 2015 helped fix the timing.

alternatives.label: Impact or comet
alternatives.text: Dallas Abbott and colleagues reported nickel- and copper-bearing spherules in an ice core, suggesting an impact may have contributed; most researchers emphasise volcanism (minority view).

alternatives.label: Myth echoes
alternatives.text: Some writers link the darkness to later legends (e.g. Fimbulwinter before Ragnarök or Arthurian dates); such links are speculative.

entries.title: Anansi the spider
entries.dateNote: Living oral tradition; date schematic (spread with the Atlantic slave trade)
entries.mainstream: Anansi is a spider trickster in Akan (Ghana) religion and folklore, associated with stories, wisdom and cunning; in one well-known tale he buys all stories from the sky god Nyame. Through the Atlantic slave trade, Anansi stories spread to the Caribbean and the Americas, where they remain widely told.

entries.title: The Rainbow Serpent
entries.dateNote: Living oral tradition; date is schematic for timeline placement
entries.mainstream: A creator being found, under many names, across many Aboriginal Australian cultures (e.g. Yurlunggur among the Yolngu of Arnhem Land). It shapes land and waterways and gives law, but can bring floods and chaos when disturbed. It appears widely in rock art.

alternatives.label: Environmental memory
alternatives.text: Some researchers relate Rainbow Serpent imagery to seasonal monsoon floods or to post-glacial sea-level rise; these are interpretive readings.

entries.title: Māui the trickster demigod
entries.dateNote: Pan-Polynesian tradition; date schematic (Aotearoa settlement c. 1300)
entries.mainstream: Across Polynesia, Māui is a culture hero and trickster who steals fire, slows the sun with snares, and fishes up land. In Māori tradition the North Island of New Zealand is Te Ika-a-Māui, "the fish of Māui", hauled up with a hook made from his grandmother's jawbone.

alternatives.label: Island-finding memory
alternatives.text: Some writers read "fishing up islands" as a poetic memory of voyagers discovering new islands (interpretive).

entries.title: Pele, goddess of Kīlauea
entries.dateNote: Tradition older; oral history linked to eruptions from c. 1410
entries.mainstream: In Hawaiian religion Pele is the goddess of volcanoes and fire, said to have voyaged from Kahiki (Tahiti) and to live in Halemaʻumaʻu crater at Kīlauea. Volcanologists dated a major Kīlauea eruption around 1410, the first mentioned in Native Hawaiian oral history, with the 60-year ʻAilāʻau eruption ending around 1470.

alternatives.label: Chants as eruption records
alternatives.text: A 2008 study by volcanologists argued that Pele and Hiʻiaka traditions describe about 400 years of real Kīlauea activity, including major lava flows and summit collapse.

alternatives.label: Living deity
alternatives.text: For many Hawaiians Pele is a living presence, not only a symbol; this is a religious view rather than a testable claim.

sources.title: Hawaiian oral tradition describes 400 years of volcanic activity at Kīlauea

entries.title: The Five Suns (Aztec world ages)
entries.dateNote: Late Postclassic Aztec form; older Mesoamerican roots
entries.mainstream: In Nahua and Aztec belief the world has been created and destroyed four times; each age, or "Sun", ended in catastrophe. In one version the fourth sun, ruled by the water goddess Chalchiuhtlicue, ended in a great flood that turned people into fish. We live in the Fifth Sun, fated to end in earthquakes. The Aztec Sun Stone is commonly interpreted as depicting the five suns.

alternatives.label: Memory of real catastrophes
alternatives.text: Some writers link the world-ages to real floods, eruptions or impacts (speculative).

alternatives.label: Cross-cultural pattern
alternatives.text: Cyclic world ages also appear in Hindu yugas, Hesiod's ages and Maya creation stories; diffusion versus independent invention is debated.

media.title: The Aztec myth of the unlikeliest sun god - Kay Almere Read

entries.title: El Dorado and the Muisca raft
entries.dateNote: Spanish reach Muisca lands 1537; raft found 1969
entries.mainstream: The legend began in 16th-century Spanish accounts of a "Golden One", a Muisca ruler who covered himself in gold dust and washed it off in a sacred lake, linked to Lake Guatavita in Colombia. It grew into the myth of a lost city of gold that drove many failed expeditions. In 1969 a gold Muisca votive raft showing a chief on a raft was found in a cave near Pasca.

alternatives.label: Kernel of truth
alternatives.text: Many scholars consider the Guatavita offering ceremony real, so the legend may be a story with a true core that was exaggerated into a lost golden city.

entries.changed: 16th–18th c.: hunted as a city of gold. 1969: Muisca raft supports the ritual behind the legend.
