entries.title: Dangun, grandson of heaven, and his "found" tomb
entries.dateNote: Traditional founding date 2333 BCE (Tongguk t'onggam, 1485); North Korea says early 30th century BCE
entries.mainstream: Korea's founding myth, first recorded in the 13th-century Samguk yusa: Hwanung, son of the Lord of Heaven Hwanin, descended to a sacred mountain with 3,000 followers and ministers of cloud, rain and wind, and taught laws, medicine and agriculture. A bear that endured 100 days in a cave on mugwort and garlic became a woman, and their son Dangun founded Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom, traditionally in 2333 BCE. National Foundation Day (3 October) celebrates it in South Korea, which counted years in the Dangi era until 1961.

alternatives.label: Real tomb (North Korean claim)
alternatives.text: After Kim Il Sung insisted Dangun was a historical person, North Korean archaeologists announced in October 1993 that they had found his tomb near Pyongyang, with bones of a man and a woman dated by electron spin resonance to over 5,011 years ago; a stone step pyramid was built over it in 1994. North Korea now treats the myth as history.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Outside observers consider the data compromised by politics and nationalism; no independent testing has been allowed. A nail of the Goguryeo period (37 BCE–668 CE) was found, and South Korean historians think it more likely the tomb of a Goguryeo-era regional leader.

alternatives.label: Symbolic reading
alternatives.text: Scholars often read the bear and tiger as two tribes seeking the favour of a heavenly prince, and the myth as an ideology of Gojoseon kingship.

entries.changed: 13th century: earliest written version (Samguk yusa). 1993: North Korea announces Dangun's tomb. 1994: mausoleum pyramid built.

entries.title: Cheomseongdae star-gazing tower
entries.dateNote: Built during the reign of Queen Seondeok (632–647)
entries.mainstream: A 9.17 m stone tower in Gyeongju, South Korea, built in the Silla kingdom under Queen Seondeok (r. 632–647). Its name means "star-gazing tower", and it is often described as the oldest surviving astronomical observatory in Asia, possibly the world. A square base of 12 stones supports a curved cylindrical body with a square window halfway up and a square top; an observation device is presumed to have stood on top. It is part of the Gyeongju Historic Areas UNESCO World Heritage Site and now tilts slightly to the north-east.

alternatives.label: Calendar symbolism (interpretation)
alternatives.text: The body is said to use 365 cut stones, one per day of the year, and the window divides it into 12 courses above and below, read as months and the 24 solar terms; the 12 base stones may also stand for months.

alternatives.label: Counting dispute
alternatives.text: Documents report different numbers of stones; a 1962 survey by Hong Sa-jun counted 366, so the "365" symbolism depends on how stones are counted.

entries.title: Lady Dai (Xin Zhui): the soft-skinned mummy
entries.dateNote: Died 169 or 168 BCE; tomb found 1968–71, excavated from 1972
entries.mainstream: Xin Zhui, Marchioness of Dai, wife of the chancellor of the Changsha Kingdom in the Western Han dynasty, died about 169 or 168 BCE aged about 50. Her tomb at Mawangdui, Changsha, found by workers digging an air-raid shelter near a hospital and excavated from January 1972 with the help of over 1,500 local high-school students, held four nested coffins, about 1,400 artefacts and more than 150 kinds of food. Her body is one of the best-preserved ever found: skin still soft and moist, joints flexible, organs and blood vessels intact with traces of type A blood. An autopsy found arteriosclerosis, gallstones, schistosomiasis and 130 melon seeds in her digestive tract, showing she died in summer within hours of eating melon.

alternatives.label: How was she preserved?
alternatives.text: Scientists point to careful preparation, airtight nested coffins and a deep chamber sealed with charcoal and white clay, which kept water and air out and the temperature cool; an acidic liquid containing salt and magnesium surrounded the body, possibly from the body itself. They do not know for certain which combination of factors worked.

alternatives.label: Not unique
alternatives.text: Other "Mawangdui-type" bodies have been found in China (Sui Xiaoyuan in Jingzhou, Ling Huiping in Lianyungang), also in liquid-filled coffins, but no consistent explanation fits all of them.

entries.title: The hidden Imperial Regalia of Japan
entries.dateNote: Used in enthronements since 690; legendary origin in the age of the gods
entries.mainstream: The Three Sacred Treasures of Japan: the sword Kusanagi no Tsurugi, the mirror Yata no Kagami and the jewel Yasakani no Magatama. Since 690 their presentation to the emperor has been central to the enthronement, but the ceremony is not public and by tradition the objects are seen only by the emperor and certain priests. They are commonly thought to be kept at Atsuta Shrine (sword), the Imperial Palace sanctuaries (jewel) and Ise Grand Shrine (mirror). Their actual historical status is unknown because they are deliberately kept from view; even at the enthronements of 1990 and 2019 they stayed shrouded in packages or boxes. In July 1945 Emperor Hirohito ordered them protected "at all costs" and said he was ready to share their fate.

alternatives.label: Divine origin (legend)
alternatives.text: The sun goddess Amaterasu gave them to her grandson Ninigi when sending him to pacify Japan, and they passed to the first emperor, Jimmu. The mirror and jewel lured Amaterasu out of the cave where she had hidden and plunged the world into darkness; the sword was taken from the tail of the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi.

alternatives.label: Lost and replaced?
alternatives.text: The six-year-old Emperor Antoku and the regalia went into the sea at the Battle of Dan-no-ura (1185). Medieval texts disagree whether the sword was lost, was already a replica, or returned by supernatural means; replicas of the sword and mirror are known from as early as the 9th century.

entries.title: Laguna Copperplate Inscription
entries.mainstream: The oldest known document from the Philippines: a copper plate about 20 × 30 cm, found in 1987 by a labourer dredging sand near the mouth of the Lumbang River in Lumban, Laguna. It is dated to the Shaka year 822, which corresponds to Monday 21 April 900 CE, and certifies that the children of one Namwaran were released from a debt of gold (1 kati and 8 suwarnas, about 865 g). Written mostly in Old Malay in the Kawi script, with Sanskrit technical words and Old Javanese or Old Tagalog honorifics, it names the polity of Tondo (Tundun) and other places. Sold to an antique dealer and then to the National Museum, it was translated by Dutch anthropologist Antoon Postma in 1991.

alternatives.label: Javanese link?
alternatives.text: Some historians link the toponym Medang (Mdang) to the Medang palace in Java; others note it is a common Malayo-Polynesian term. Postma himself left open that Mdang and Tondo might originally be Javanese place names.

alternatives.label: Local places
alternatives.text: The Pila Historical Society Foundation and historian Jaime Tiongson argue that Pailah and Puliran refer to places near where the plate was found, citing a large precolonial settlement at Pila.

alternatives.label: Precolonial knowledge
alternatives.text: It is the earliest evidence of mathematics in precolonial Philippine societies: a standard system of weights for gold and a date fixed by the phases of the Moon.

entries.changed: 1987: found while dredging. 1991: translated by Antoon Postma; it is now the oldest known document from the Philippines and a key source on 10th-century polities such as Tondo.

entries.title: The Tasaday: Stone Age tribe or hoax?
entries.mainstream: In 1971 Manuel Elizalde, head of the Philippine minorities agency PANAMIN and a crony of President Ferdinand Marcos, announced the discovery of the Tasaday, a small group in the rainforest of Mindanao said to live in caves with "Stone Age" tools in complete isolation. National Geographic covered them (cover story, August 1972), and visitors included Charles Lindbergh and Gina Lollobrigida. In 1972 Marcos declared a 77 km² reserve around their caves, and in 1976, under martial law, closed it to all visitors; no anthropologist had studied them for more than six weeks. Elizalde fled the country in 1983 amid allegations that he squandered foundation money.

alternatives.label: Hoax (1986 claim)
alternatives.text: After Marcos fell in 1986, Swiss journalist Oswald Iten and Joey Lozano made an unauthorised two-hour visit, found the caves deserted and claimed the Tasaday were members of known local tribes who had posed as cave-dwellers under pressure from Elizalde; some local people admitted pretending to be Tasaday for money and goods.

alternatives.label: Genuine but recent isolation
alternatives.text: Linguist Lawrence Reid, after ten months of fieldwork (1993–1996), concluded they "probably were as isolated as they claim", unfamiliar with agriculture, with a distinct dialect, and that the original reporters perpetrated no hoax; he estimated their isolation lasted perhaps no more than 150 years. A widely held summary is that they were a separate forest-gathering group rarely in contact with neighbours, but not a Stone Age survival.

entries.changed: 1971–72: hailed as a "Stone Age" tribe. 1986: denounced as a hoax. 1990s: linguistic work supports a real, recently isolated group.

entries.title: Iram of the Pillars and Ubar, "Atlantis of the Sands"
entries.dateNote: Named in the Quran (7th century CE); the city or people it refers to are undated
entries.mainstream: The Quran (Surah 89) mentions "Iram, who had lofty pillars" alongside the destroyed people of ʿĀd; later the Thousand and One Nights tells of the many-columned city of Iram. Ubar, a legendary land of southern Arabia, is often equated with it and nicknamed the Atlantis of the Sands. Interpretations range from a city (Alexandria, Damascus, or a city that moved) to a region (the biblical Aram) or a tribe whose "pillars" were tent poles. Inscriptions at the Temple of al-Lat at Wadi Ramm in Jordan mention Iram and the tribe of ʿĀd, making it a more plausible candidate for some scholars.

alternatives.label: Found at Shisr? (Clapp)
alternatives.text: Amateur archaeologist Nicholas Clapp proposed that Iram is Ubar and identified it with the archaeological site of Shisr in Dhofar, Oman, a former oasis trading post on the frankincense routes (part of the UNESCO Land of Frankincense since 2000). Scholars generally do not accept this, and Clapp himself later denied the Shisr identification.

alternatives.label: Source of the legend
alternatives.text: Ubar is described by ancient and medieval authors as a land rather than a city; it has been suggested that the drying of the spring and abandonment of Shisr could have inspired the legend of a lost city.

entries.title: The tooth of the Buddha in Kandy
entries.dateNote: Tradition: arrived in Sri Lanka in the reign of Sirimeghavanna (301–328 CE)
entries.mainstream: Sri Lanka venerates a tooth of the Buddha at the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic (Sri Dalada Maligawa) in the former royal palace complex of Kandy, part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Tradition holds that after the Buddha's cremation his left canine was kept in Kalinga, India, and that when Kalinga was attacked Princess Hemamali and Prince Dantha carried it to Sri Lanka, hidden in her hair, in the reign of Sirimeghavanna of Anuradhapura (301–328). Because whoever held the relic was believed to hold the right to rule, kings kept it beside their palaces, moving it with each capital; it was hidden in a grinding stone at one point and carried away from Kandy during the Portuguese invasion of 1603. Today it lies within seven golden caskets and is honoured by the annual Esala Perahera procession.

alternatives.label: Destroyed in Goa? (Portuguese account)
alternatives.text: Portuguese chroniclers João de Barros and Diogo do Couto wrote that a tooth relic seized in the 1560 expedition against the Jaffna Kingdom was taken to Goa and destroyed, by burning and casting into the sea, on the viceroy Constantino de Bragança's orders.

alternatives.label: Survival (Sri Lankan tradition)
alternatives.text: The relic venerated in Kandy is held by Buddhists to be the authentic tooth; the relationship between it and the relic destroyed in Goa is a matter of differing accounts. A 2024 survey found 32 museums and temples worldwide claiming one or more Buddha tooth relics.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Relic of the tooth of the Buddha

entries.title: Mermaid mummies of Japan and the "Fiji mermaid"
entries.mainstream: Japanese tradition knows the ningyo ("human-fish"); the oldest pictures (scroll copy of 1069) show one presented to Prince Shōtoku in the 7th century, and some temples keep preserved "mermaids" tied to such legends. In the Edo period craftsmen made them commercially: a Dutch official on Dejima (1820s) saw "mermaids", two-headed men and dragons for sale. One reportedly bought from Japanese sailors in 1822 became the "Fiji mermaid" (a monkey's torso sewn to a fish), shown in London that year and by P. T. Barnum in New York in 1842. In 2022–23 researchers from Kurashiki University of Science and the Arts scanned the "mermaid mummy" of Enjuin temple, Asakuchi (Okayama), which came with a note saying it was netted off Tosa (Kōchi) between 1736 and 1740.

alternatives.label: Result of the 2023 study
alternatives.text: X-ray CT, microscopy and radiocarbon dating showed no skeleton except fish jaws and fin bones: the body is cloth, paper and cotton with plaster-like material, covered with layered paper, pufferfish skin and animal hair above and croaker-fish skin below; scales date it to the late 19th century, and no DNA was found.

alternatives.label: Real animals behind the legend?
alternatives.text: Proposed sources for ningyo lore include giant salamanders (the earliest were caught in fresh water), dugongs or Steller's sea cows, seals, and oarfish (whose red crest matches some descriptions).

entries.changed: 1822: Fiji mermaid exhibited in London. 1842: Barnum shows it in New York. 2023: CT study shows a Japanese temple mermaid is a made object of the late 1800s.

sources.title: Kurashiki University of Science and the Arts: final report on the Enjuin mermaid mummy (2023, Japanese)

entries.title: Rongorongo: the undeciphered script of Rapa Nui
entries.dateNote: Wood of one tablet dated to the mid-15th century (2024); texts collected from the 1860s
entries.mainstream: A system of glyphs on about two dozen wooden objects from Easter Island (Rapa Nui), collected in the late 19th century and now scattered among museums; none remain on the island. The glyphs (outlines of humans, animals, plants and shapes) run in reverse boustrophedon, every other line upside down. Apart from part of one tablet that relates to a lunar calendar and a possible genealogy, none can be read. Oral history says only an elite was literate and the tablets were sacred; the scribes and their knowledge were lost when Rapa Nui society collapsed after Peruvian slave raids and epidemics in the 1860s. A 2024 radiocarbon study of tablets in Rome securely dated the wood of one to the mid-15th century, though the carving could be younger.

alternatives.label: Independent invention
alternatives.text: If rongorongo is true writing and was invented on the island before European contact, it would be one of very few independent inventions of writing in human history; the 2024 date supports pre-contact use.

alternatives.label: Inspired by Europeans
alternatives.text: Others suggest the islanders created it after seeing writing during the Spanish treaty-signing visit of 1770; some tablets are carved on European oars or South African yellowwood, and the script was not reported by early explorers (possibly because it was taboo).

alternatives.label: Fanciful readings
alternatives.text: As with most undeciphered scripts, there are many fanciful interpretations and claimed translations; scholars accept none of them.

entries.changed: 1860s: tablets first reported by missionaries. 1958: Barthel publishes the corpus. 2024: radiocarbon dating suggests pre-contact origin for at least one tablet.

sources.title: The invention of writing on Rapa Nui (Easter Island). New radiocarbon dates on the Rongorongo script

entries.title: Roi Mata: a legend that led to a grave
entries.dateNote: The last Roi Mata lived around 1600; grave located in 1967
entries.mainstream: Roi Mata was a chiefly title in central Vanuatu borne by a dynasty from the 11th to the 17th century; the most famous holder, often simply called Roi Mata, lived around 1600. Oral tradition says he united the tribes, ruled peacefully, was poisoned by his brother, and was buried away from his homeland on the island of Eretoka, where his name was then avoided for fear of his spirit. In 1967 French archaeologist José Garanger used these stories to locate the grave on Eretoka: an elaborate burial with Roi Mata and over 25 members of his retinue. Three associated sites on Efate, Lelepa and Eretoka (his residence, the site of his death and the burial site) became UNESCO's Chief Roi Mata's Domain in 2008.

alternatives.label: Oral history as evidence
alternatives.text: The find shows oral tradition guiding archaeologists to a burial of about 370 years earlier, including details such as a mass burial of the chief's retinue.

entries.changed: 1967: Garanger finds the grave using oral tradition. 2008: UNESCO World Heritage listing.

entries.title: Haʻamonga ʻa Maui, the "Stonehenge of the Pacific"
entries.dateNote: Around 1200 CE (traditional history)
entries.mainstream: A coral-limestone trilithon at Niutōua on Tongatapu, Tonga: two uprights about 5.2 m high, each weighing about 30–40 tonnes above ground, with a lintel set into deep mortises. Historical analysis places it around 1200 CE under Tuʻitātui, the eleventh Tuʻi Tonga, probably as a gateway to the royal compound, representing his two sons joined by the lintel. Nearby is a stone "throne" the king leaned against to avoid being attacked from behind. A national park since 1972.

alternatives.label: Built by Māui (tradition)
alternatives.text: Traditional accounts say the hero Māui made it, carrying the stones from ʻUvea in a giant canoe, as they were too big for mortals; its name means "the burden of Māui". Some believe it points to Pulotu, the land of the gods.

alternatives.label: Solar calendar?
alternatives.text: In 1967 King Taufaʻahau Tupou IV concluded it marked the sunrise at the solstices and equinoxes, a view supported by historian Tevita Fale, who described a V-shaped mark on the lintel aligned with these sunrises.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Astronomer Kik Velt of ʻAtenisi Institute argued the V-mark is only about 10 cm long and points along the lintel's main axis, too short to be a reliable direction marker.

entries.title: The Seven Sisters and the lost Pleiad
entries.dateNote: Proposed origin about 100,000 years ago (speculative); recorded versions are much later
entries.mainstream: Many cultures call the Pleiades star cluster the "seven sisters" although most people see six stars, and many tell a story to explain the missing seventh. In Greek myth the Pleiades are daughters of Atlas, turned into stars to escape the hunter Orion; one sister went into hiding. Across Aboriginal Australia the cluster is a group of young women pursued by a man or men in Orion, and one sister has died, hidden or been abducted. Folklorist Stith Thompson noted the cluster is "nearly always imagined" as seven sisters. The cluster appears on the Nebra sky disc and heads Babylonian star lists, and Japan's 8th-century Kojiki calls it Mutsuraboshi, "six stars".

alternatives.label: 100,000-year-old story (Norris & Norris)
alternatives.text: Astronomers Ray and Barnaby Norris (2021) used Gaia star motions to show that about 100,000 years ago the star Pleione was farther from Atlas and easy to see, so the cluster would have shown seven stars; they suggest the stories could date back to before modern humans left Africa, which would make them perhaps the oldest stories on Earth.

alternatives.label: European diffusion (older view)
alternatives.text: Anthropologists once thought Europeans brought the Greek story to Australia, where it was adapted; Norris notes the Aboriginal stories appear much older than European contact.

alternatives.label: Independent origins (interpretation)
alternatives.text: Because the cluster is a conspicuous group of six or so stars, similar stories could also have arisen independently in different cultures; the deep-time explanation remains a hypothesis.

entries.title: Menehune: Hawaiʻi's hidden builders
entries.dateNote: Traditions recorded from the 19th century; 1820 census claim
entries.mainstream: In Hawaiian tradition the Menehune are a race of small, dwarf-like people who live hidden in deep forests and valleys and are superb craftspeople, said to have lived in Hawaiʻi before settlers came from elsewhere in Polynesia. They work only at night and abandon any project not finished by dawn; only their children and people connected to them can see them. Structures attributed to them include the Alekoko (Menehune) fishpond wall at Niumalu and the Kīkīaola ditch at Waimea on Kauaʻi, structures on Necker Island and Ulupō Heiau on Oʻahu.

alternatives.label: Remembered first settlers
alternatives.text: Some early scholars proposed a first settlement from the Marquesas and a second from Tahiti, whose newcomers oppressed the "commoners" (manahune in Tahitian), who fled to the mountains; supporters cite a census of Kauaʻi ordered by Kaumualiʻi around 1820 that listed 65 people as menehune.

alternatives.label: Post-contact legend
alternatives.text: Folklorist Katharine Luomala argued the small-people legends are a post-European adaptation of the term manahune ("lowly people") to European tales of brownies; others reply that absence from early records proves little for an oral tradition.

entries.title: The Kaimanawa "wall"
entries.mainstream: A line of block-like stones in the Kaimanawa State Forest south of Lake Taupō, New Zealand. In May 1996 the NZ Listener and the Holmes TV show featured archaeologist and historian Barry Brailsford's view that it was "the best evidence so far" of a pre-Māori "Waitaha nation" settled 2,000 years ago, because nothing like it exists in Māori culture. Department of Conservation archaeologist Neville Ritchie examined it on 7 May 1996 and found matching micro-irregularities across the joints and imperfect joint alignments, showing the "blocks" were one rock. Geologist Peter Wood identified it as jointed Rangitaiki ignimbrite, a 330,000-year-old volcanic rock that cracks this way as it cools.

alternatives.label: Pre-Māori civilisation (claim)
alternatives.text: The idea that the wall was built by an earlier culture remains popular in alternative literature; Tūwharetoa people refer to the place in oral tradition as a kōhatu (rock).

alternatives.label: Natural formation (finding)
alternatives.text: Both specialists who inspected it found no evidence of human working; Te Ara, the encyclopedia of New Zealand, describes it as a natural phenomenon.

entries.changed: May 1996: claimed as a megalith; within weeks archaeological and geological inspections conclude it is natural ignimbrite.

sources.title: Te Ara: The Kaimanawa wall (Ideas about Māori origins, K. R. Howe)
Ritchie, N. A. (1996). A New Age Myth: the Kaimanawa Wall. NZ Skeptics

entries.title: The bunyip
entries.dateNote: Oral tradition of unknown age; first printed 1812
entries.mainstream: A creature of Aboriginal tradition in south-eastern Australia said to lurk in swamps, billabongs, creeks and waterholes; the word comes from the Wemba-Wemba or Wergaia language of Victoria and is often translated today as "devil" or "evil spirit". At least nine regional variants are known. "Bahnyip" first appeared in print in the Sydney Gazette in 1812, describing a large black seal-like animal with a terrible voice. An outline of a speared bunyip about 11 paces long, cut into a creek bank at Challicum near Ararat, Victoria, was recorded in 1851 and reportedly retraced by Aboriginal people each year until the mid-1850s. Colonial newspapers reported bunyip fossils (Geelong, 1845) and a "bunyip skull" from the Murrumbidgee (1846), which experts including Richard Owen identified in 1847 as the deformed foetal skull of a foal or calf.

alternatives.label: Memory of megafauna
alternatives.text: George Bennett of the Australian Museum (1871) proposed that bunyip stories recall extinct marsupials such as Diprotodon; Pat Vickers-Rich and Neil Archbold (1990s) cautiously agreed that legends may stem from encounters with fossil bones or even living prehistoric animals, noting that Aboriginal people often identified such remains as bunyips.

alternatives.label: Seals, birds and other animals
alternatives.text: Charles Fenner (1933) suggested seals that swam far up the Murray and Darling; others point to the booming call of the Australasian bittern ("bunyip bird") or, from an 1845 description with pale blue eggs and a bright chest, the southern cassowary (Karl Brandt, 2017).

alternatives.label: Spirit being
alternatives.text: Many accounts treat the bunyip as a spirit rather than an animal; some modern sources suggest a linguistic link to the creator being Bunjil.

entries.title: Pakal's tomb and the "astronaut" lid
entries.mainstream: Kʼinich Janaabʼ Pakal ruled the Maya city of Palenque from age 12 in 615 until his death on 29 August 683, a reign of 68 years. In 1948 Mexican archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier lifted a floor slab in the Temple of the Inscriptions and found a rubble-filled stairway; clearing it took four years, and in 1952 he reached Pakal's tomb with its huge carved sarcophagus. The lid shows Pakal between the heavens and the underworld: above him a cruciform world tree with a celestial bird and serpent, below him the jaws of the underworld, with sun, moon and star signs and six ancestors around the edges. The tomb has since been resealed. An underground water channel beneath the temple was found in 2016 and a stucco mask of an elderly Pakal in 2018.

alternatives.label: Ancient astronaut (von Däniken)
alternatives.text: In Chariots of the Gods? (1968) Erich von Däniken reproduced the lid (mislabelled as from Copán), compared Pakal's pose with Mercury astronauts and read the motifs below him as rocket exhaust, as possible evidence of extraterrestrial influence.

alternatives.label: Maya iconography (mainstream)
alternatives.text: Archaeologists, epigraphers and art historians almost universally reject this, noting that the claim relies on visual impression alone and ignores Maya artistic conventions, cosmology and the accompanying texts, which identify the scene as the king and the world tree.

alternatives.label: Whose bones?
alternatives.text: Low tooth wear first suggested the skeleton was about 40 years younger than the 80-year-old king of the inscriptions; later skeletal analysis supports an age in the eighth or ninth decade, consistent with the texts (a softer elite diet would explain the teeth).

entries.changed: 1952: tomb found. 1968: von Däniken's astronaut reading. 1973 onwards: decipherment of Palenque's dynastic texts confirms Pakal's identity and dates.

sources.title: Pre-Hispanic City and National Park of Palenque (UNESCO)

entries.title: The Lord of Sipán: a royal tomb saved from looters
entries.dateNote: Moche period; the burial platform was built before c. 300 CE; found 1987
entries.mainstream: In early 1987 looters digging at Huaca Rajada, an adobe pyramid and platform complex near Sipán in the Lambayeque Valley of northern Peru, found gold objects; a quarrel among them led police to raid the site and call archaeologist Walter Alva. His team found the intact tomb of a Moche ruler, now called the Lord of Sipán: a man about 1.63 m tall, aged 35–45, with gold, silver and copper headdresses, a face mask, a gold pectoral (a man's head with an octopus body) and necklaces of gold and silver peanut-shaped beads (gold on the right for the sun, silver on the left for the moon). Buried with him were three young women, two men (with amputated feet), a child, a dog and 451 offerings; another man sat in a niche above. By 2007 fourteen tombs had been identified. The Royal Tombs of Sipán Museum opened in 2002.

alternatives.label: Significance
alternatives.text: Archaeologists consider it one of the most important finds in South America in the late 20th century because the main tomb was untouched by grave robbers, giving a rare complete view of Moche royal burial.

alternatives.label: The retinue
alternatives.text: The three women apparently died some time before the burial; the warriors' feet were amputated, as if, in the excavators' reading, to prevent them from leaving the tomb.

entries.title: Breaking the Maya code
entries.mainstream: Maya script is the only Mesoamerican writing system that has been substantially deciphered. The earliest identifiable inscriptions date to the 3rd century BCE (San Bartolo, Chakjobon), and it was used until the Spanish conquest. It combines logograms with syllabic signs. As part of his campaign against "pagan" rites, Bishop Diego de Landa ordered Maya books collected and destroyed; only three codices were long known to survive, with the Grolier Codex authenticated as a fourth in 2015. Yet Landa also recorded a supposed Maya "alphabet" that became a key to decipherment. By 2008 the sound of about 80% of Maya writing could be read and the meaning of about 60% understood.

alternatives.label: Old school: calendar priests
alternatives.text: For much of the 20th century leading scholars such as J. Eric S. Thompson held that the inscriptions were mainly calendrical, astronomical and religious, and that the script was not phonetic.

alternatives.label: Knorozov and the phonetic breakthrough
alternatives.text: In 1952 Soviet scholar Yuri Knorozov argued that Landa's "alphabet" was really syllabic; many Western Mayanists dismissed him, partly because Soviet editors added Marxist-Leninist claims. In 1959 Tatiana Proskouriakoff showed that date patterns at Piedras Negras recorded the lives of rulers, and at the 1973 Palenque round table Linda Schele, Floyd Lounsbury and Peter Mathews reconstructed most of Palenque's king list in an afternoon.

entries.changed: 1952: Knorozov proposes syllabic reading. 1958: Berlin identifies emblem glyphs. 1959: Proskouriakoff finds dynastic history. 1973: Palenque king list reconstructed. 1986: "The Blood of Kings" exhibition helps turn the field. 2015: Grolier Codex authenticated.

entries.title: Chichen Itza: the serpent of light and the chirping pyramid
entries.dateNote: Built sometime between the 8th and 12th centuries CE
entries.mainstream: El Castillo, the Temple of Kukulcán at Chichen Itza in Yucatán, was built by the Maya sometime between the 8th and 12th centuries over an earlier substructure, as a temple to the feathered serpent Kukulcán (related to the Aztec Quetzalcoatl). Plumed serpent sculptures run down the northern balustrade. Around the spring and autumn equinoxes the late-afternoon sun casts triangular shadows on the north-west balustrade, creating the illusion of a serpent crawling down the pyramid, watched by thousands each spring. Handclaps in front of the staircase return a descending "chirped" echo.

alternatives.label: Designed alignment?
alternatives.text: It is not known whether the serpent of light was purposeful design, since the effect can be seen with little change for several weeks around the equinoxes.

alternatives.label: Intentional acoustics? (speculative)
alternatives.text: Acoustician David Lubman modelled the chirp as diffraction from the stair treads and speculated that the staircase was deliberately designed to imitate the call of the quetzal bird; others (e.g. Declercq et al. 2004) analysed the effect physically without assuming intent.

sources.title: A theoretical study of special acoustic effects caused by the staircase of the El Castillo pyramid at the Maya ruins of Chichen-Itza in Mexico

entries.title: Aztlán, the lost homeland of the Aztecs
entries.dateNote: Departure dated 1064–65 in the Anales de Tlatelolco (2004 translation)
entries.mainstream: Aztlán ("Aztec" means "people from Aztlán") is the homeland from which the Mexica and other Nahua peoples were said to have migrated to central Mexico, where the Mexica later founded Tenochtitlan. Accounts tell of seven tribes emerging from Chicomoztoc, the Place of the Seven Caves, and of an island in a "Lake of the Moon". Some describe a paradise, others (Codex Aubin) a tyranny under the Azteca Chicomoztoca; guided by their priest and the god Huitzilopochtli, who told them to call themselves Mexica, they left. A 2004 translation of the Anales de Tlatelolco gives the only known date for the departure: 4 Eagle in the year 1 Flint (1064–65).

alternatives.label: Real place?
alternatives.text: Historians tend to place Aztlán in north-western Mexico or the south-western United States; since the 1960s Mexican scholars have considered the island town of Mexcaltitán de Uribe in Nayarit, an idea still debated. Others think it impossible to locate because the accounts conflict, or regard it as mythological.

alternatives.label: A royal search
alternatives.text: Friar Diego Durán wrote that Moctezuma I sent warriors and sages to find Aztlán and that they succeeded; Durán wrote after the conquest, before accurate maps existed.

alternatives.label: Sky sign
alternatives.text: One reconstruction links the start of the migration to the 1054 "guest star" supernova (see SN 1054). In 1969 the poet Alurista made Aztlán a symbol of Chicano identity in El Plan Espiritual de Aztlán.

entries.title: The Great Law of Peace and the darkened sun
entries.dateNote: Disputed: 1142 or 1451 eclipse; other estimates up to c. 1600
entries.mainstream: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) oral history tells that the Great Peacemaker (Deganawida), with Hiawatha and Jigonhsasee, united the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca under the Great Law of Peace (Gayanashagowa), an oral constitution recorded on wampum belts. Jigonhsasee became the first Clan Mother, and clan mothers chose the chiefs. One account says that fighting among the Seneca, the last nation to join, stopped when the sun darkened and day seemed to turn to night. Since William Canfield's Legends of the Iroquois (1902) scholars have asked whether this was a solar eclipse that could date the founding.

alternatives.label: 1451 eclipse (majority view)
alternatives.text: Most scholars have favoured the solar eclipse of 1451 as the likely founding date, consistent with archaeology; in 1982 Dean Snow argued the evidence did not support any date before 1350.

alternatives.label: 1142 eclipse (Mann and Fields)
alternatives.text: Barbara Mann and Jerry Fields (1997) argued the 1451 eclipse is a poor fit and that the eclipse of 31 August 1142 matches the tradition; by 2007–08 reviews regarded 1142 as possible, though most still saw 1451 as the safer choice.

alternatives.label: Caution
alternatives.text: A few scholars question dating the confederacy from the eclipse story at all; overall estimates range from the 12th century to the 15th century or later. In 1988 the US Congress formally recognised the confederacy's influence on the US Constitution.

sources.title: A Sign in the Sky: Dating the League of the Haudenosaunee

entries.title: The Thunderbird
entries.dateNote: Depictions date back about 4,000 years
entries.mainstream: A powerful bird-like spirit in the traditions of many North American Indigenous peoples, especially on the Pacific Northwest Coast but also in the Southwest, Great Lakes, Great Plains and East. In Algonquian tellings it makes thunder by flapping its wings and lightning by flashing its eyes (also among the Iroquois), ruling the upper world and fighting the underwater panther or Great Horned Serpent of the underworld. Depictions of thunderbirds are found at sites dating back about 4,000 years, such as petroglyphs at Twin Bluffs, Wisconsin. Pacific coast peoples tell of struggles between Thunderbird and Whale.

alternatives.label: Earthquake memory
alternatives.text: Researchers have examined whether Thunderbird and Whale stories relate to the Cascadia earthquake of 1700 (see entry).

alternatives.label: Fossils and extinct birds
alternatives.text: Historian Adrienne Mayor and Tom Holland have suggested the stories may draw on discoveries of pterosaur fossils; anthropologist Paulette Steeves suggests memories of the extinct giant bird Teratornis.

alternatives.label: Cryptid sightings
alternatives.text: "Thunderbird" is also used for alleged modern sightings of giant condor- or pterosaur-like birds, including a supposedly lost 19th-century photograph; scientists attribute such sightings to misidentified known animals. Indigenous traditions hold that the Thunderbird is a spirit, not a physical animal.

entries.title: The Lost Colony of Roanoke and "CROATOAN"
entries.mainstream: In 1587 English settlers under John White landed on Roanoke Island (now North Carolina), meant for the Chesapeake Bay but left there by pilot Simon Fernandes. White sailed home for supplies; war with Spain delayed his return until August 1590, when he found the settlement fortified but abandoned, with "CRO" carved into a tree and "CROATOAN" into the palisade, which he took to mean the colonists had moved to Croatoan Island. Storms and a lost anchor forced his ships home. Among the missing was his infant granddaughter Virginia Dare, born in the colony.

alternatives.label: Absorbed into Native communities
alternatives.text: Speculation that the colonists joined nearby peoples appears as early as 1605; John Lawson (1701–09) met Hatteras people who said some ancestors were white and some had grey eyes.

alternatives.label: Killed
alternatives.text: Jamestown sources reported that Wahunsenacawh (Chief Powhatan) had massacred them; William Strachey wrote that a few survived. The source of the claim is unknown, and after 1622 it was used in propaganda to justify war on the Powhatan.

alternatives.label: Drought
alternatives.text: A 1998 tree-ring study (Stahle, Blanton et al.) found the worst growing season in 800 years in 1587, within an extreme drought of 1587–89, which could have caused famine and conflict.

entries.changed: 1590: colony found deserted. 1834: George Bancroft makes Virginia Dare a national legend. 1998: drought identified from tree rings. Excavations continue.

entries.title: Shag Harbour UFO incident (Canada, 1967)
entries.mainstream: On the night of 4 October 1967, at about 11:20 pm, at least eleven people saw a low-flying lit object head toward the water off Shag Harbour, a fishing village in Nova Scotia; witnesses heard a whistling "like a bomb", a whoosh and a bang. Laurie Wickens and four friends saw it floating 250–300 m offshore and reported a plane crash; RCMP officers watched it before it sank, still lit. Fishing boats and a Coast Guard cutter found no survivors or debris, and the Halifax rescue centre found no aircraft missing. Earlier that evening an Air Canada crew over Quebec, a fishing-boat captain with radar returns and people around Halifax had reported strange lights.

alternatives.label: Officially unidentified
alternatives.text: Because conventional explanations such as aircraft and flares had been dismissed, the rescue centre labelled it a "UFO Report"; navy divers searched the seabed for three days and found nothing. Canada's Department of National Defence files and the US Condon Committee record the case.

alternatives.label: Underwater craft (1990s claim)
alternatives.text: From 1993 ufologist Chris Styles and a co-author (in the book Dark Object) claimed the object travelled underwater to a naval sonar facility near Shelburne and was joined by a second craft before both left; no evidence for this has been presented.

alternatives.label: Flares or a fireball (sceptical view)
alternatives.text: Brian Dunning (Skeptoid, 2017) notes the earliest newspaper accounts describe only a few lights descending and one floating briefly, and argues that marine distress flares or a fragmenting meteor fireball fit the reports; he reads the Coast Guard telex ("flares, etc. checked - nil results") as finding no evidence, not ruling flares out.

entries.title: Snowball Earth: when the planet froze over?
entries.dateNote: Sturtian c. 717–660 Ma; Marinoan c. 650–635 Ma
entries.mainstream: A hypothesis that during the Cryogenian Period Earth's surface froze nearly entirely, in two major glacial episodes: the Sturtian (c. 717–660 million years ago) and the Marinoan (c. 650–635 million years ago). It explains glacial deposits laid down at tropical palaeolatitudes, banded iron formations and the "cap carbonates" (thick limestone or dolomite layers) that sit sharply on top of the glacial beds. Joseph Kirschvink coined the term in 1992 and proposed the escape mechanism: volcanic CO2 building up until an ultra-greenhouse melted the ice. Paul Hoffman and colleagues revived the idea in Science in 1998 using rocks in Namibia. The episodes came shortly before the Avalon and Cambrian radiations of multicellular life.

alternatives.label: Hard snowball
alternatives.text: Proponents argue a fully frozen ocean best explains low-latitude glacial deposits, cap carbonates and isotopic shifts.

alternatives.label: Slushball Earth
alternatives.text: A competing view holds that a thin equatorial band of open (or seasonally open) water remained, which would make it easier for life to survive and for the planet to escape the icehouse.

alternatives.label: Sceptics
alternatives.text: Opponents contest the geological evidence for global glaciation and the physical feasibility of an all-ice ocean; as of 2007 only one "very reliable" (still challenged) data point identified tropical tillites, and some cap carbonates may instead reflect methane release.

entries.changed: 1871 onward: ancient glacial deposits found in Scotland, Australia, India and Norway. Douglas Mawson speculated about global glaciation but assumed fixed continents. 1964: W. Brian Harland shows tillites in Svalbard and Greenland formed at tropical latitudes. 1992: Kirschvink coins "snowball Earth". 1998: Hoffman et al. bring it to wide attention. 2010: Macdonald et al. report evidence that the Sturtian glaciation reached sea level near the equator.

entries.title: Lomekwi 3: stone tools older than humans
entries.mainstream: In July 2011 a team led by Sonia Harmand and Jason Lewis took a wrong turn near Lake Turkana, Kenya, and found stone artefacts at a site they named Lomekwi 3. About 20 excavated artefacts (anvils, cores and flakes, one flake refitting to its core) and about 130 surface finds were dated, from volcanic ash layers and magnetic reversals, to 3.3 million years ago – about 700,000 years older than the Gona tools of Ethiopia and roughly 500,000 years older than the genus Homo. The tools are large (the biggest weighs 15 kg) and were assigned to a new tradition, the "Lomekwian". Published in Nature in May 2015.

alternatives.label: Who made them
alternatives.text: Because they predate Homo, the makers may have been Australopithecus or Kenyanthropus (found nearby); it is unclear whether the technology is ancestral to later Homo tools or was forgotten and reinvented.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Some researchers (e.g. Domínguez-Rodrigo and colleagues, 2019) have questioned whether the artefacts were securely in their original layer, and so the 3.3-million-year age; independent researchers who examined the tools were generally supportive of Harmand's conclusions.

alternatives.label: Invisible older tool use
alternatives.text: Primate studies suggest a still older, archaeologically almost invisible "organic tool age" of plant and percussive tools may have come first.

entries.title: Turkana Boy (Nariokotome Boy)
entries.dateNote: 1.5–1.6 million years ago
entries.mainstream: KNM-WT 15000, a nearly complete skeleton (108 bones) of a Homo erectus (or Homo ergaster) youth who lived 1.5–1.6 million years ago, found in 1984 by Kamoya Kimeu by the Nariokotome River near Lake Turkana, Kenya. It is the most complete Homo erectus skeleton ever found. He was tall for his age, with a narrow pelvis suited to fully terrestrial walking and a body shape that would shed heat under a hot sun, but kept a low forehead, strong brow ridges and no chin; brain size was about 880 cc.

alternatives.label: How old was he?
alternatives.text: Walker and Leakey (1993) estimated 11–12 years from bone maturity; later work assuming a less human-like growth pattern suggests about 8; overall estimates range from 7 to 11, which also changes estimates of his adult height.

alternatives.label: Speech
alternatives.text: Whether his anatomy allowed human-like speech has been debated.

entries.title: Dmanisi: the first humans outside Africa?
entries.dateNote: 1.85–1.77 million years ago
entries.mainstream: Fossils and stone tools from Dmanisi in Georgia (southern Caucasus) date to 1.85–1.77 million years ago, making them the earliest well-dated hominin fossils in Eurasia. Over a hundred postcranial bones and five well-preserved skulls (Dmanisi Skulls 1–5) show a mosaic: essentially modern legs for long-distance walking, but small bodies (145–166 cm) and small brains (545–775 cc) closer to Homo habilis, with ape-like arms. Their small size challenged the idea that only large-brained, tall Homo erectus could leave Africa.

alternatives.label: One variable species
alternatives.text: The Dmanisi team (Lordkipanidze et al., 2013, describing the complete Skull 5) argue all the skulls belong to one population with large age and sex differences, implying early Homo species named from African fossils may be one variable lineage.

alternatives.label: Several species
alternatives.text: Others disagree; a massive jaw (D2600) was made the type of a separate species, Homo georgicus, in 2002, and a 2014 comment in Science disputed the single-species reading. The name is still debated.

entries.title: Peking Man and the fossils that vanished in 1941
entries.dateNote: Deposits c. 800,000–230,000 years ago; fossils lost December 1941
entries.mainstream: Homo erectus fossils from Zhoukoudian cave, about 50 km south-west of Beijing, appear in deposits from about 800,000 to 230,000 years ago (Shen et al. 2009 used aluminium-26/beryllium-10 burial dating, giving about 770,000 years for the lower layers). The first tooth was found in 1921 and Pei Wenzhong found a skullcap in 1929; Zhoukoudian became the most productive Homo erectus site in the world. During the Japanese occupation, the fossils of at least 40 individuals were packed into two footlockers for shipment to the American Museum of Natural History; after they left Peking Union Medical College on 4 December 1941 they were never seen again. Science survives through Franz Weidenreich's casts and descriptions.

alternatives.label: Fate of the fossils (unresolved)
alternatives.text: Rumours place them on a sunken ship (such as the Japanese Awa Maru), ground up as traditional medicine, or buried at Qinhuangdao, where a US Marine recalled finding a box of bones in 1947; Japanese and American groups have each been accused of taking them. Large rewards have produced nothing.

alternatives.label: Out of Asia vs Out of Africa
alternatives.text: In the 1920s–30s Peking Man supported a Central Asian origin of humanity and later became a symbol in Chinese national and Marxist narratives; today Out of Africa is the consensus and Peking Man is seen as an offshoot, though some interbreeding with human ancestors is still discussed.

alternatives.label: Hunters or prey?
alternatives.text: Whether Peking Man controlled fire and lived in the cave, or was killed by giant hyenas and dragged there, is debated.

sources.title: Age of Zhoukoudian Homo erectus determined with 26Al/10Be burial dating

entries.title: Apollo 11 Cave stones: Africa's oldest figurative art
entries.dateNote: Painted slabs c. 30,000 years BP
entries.mainstream: A rock shelter in the ǀAi-ǀAis/Richtersveld park of south-western Namibia (Nama name "Goachanas"), occupied in pulses from about 71,000 to 29,000 years ago. Archaeologist Wolfgang Erich Wendt named it after the Apollo 11 Moon mission, which had just returned to Earth. Seven grey-brown quartzite slabs painted with animals, radiocarbon dated to about 30,000 years BP, are among the oldest figurative art in Africa; the most famous shows a therianthrope combining human hind legs, an antelope body and horns, and a feline head. They are now in the National Museum of Namibia, Windhoek. In 2007 the site was found "severely vandalised".

alternatives.label: Shamanic interpretation
alternatives.text: Many rock-art researchers read human–animal figures in southern African art as linked to San trance experience and transformation; whether that applies to images this old is an interpretation, not something the stones themselves can prove.

alternatives.label: Hunting magic or story
alternatives.text: Other readings see the figures as hunting imagery or depictions of myth; the meaning of the composite figure is unknown.

entries.title: Tsodilo Hills and the "python stone" ritual claim
entries.dateNote: Claimed c. 70,000 years ago; paintings up to c. 24,000 years old
entries.mainstream: The Tsodilo Hills in north-west Botswana (UNESCO World Heritage, 2001) hold over 4,500 rock paintings at some 500 sites, a few dated to about 24,000 years ago, and are sacred to the San, who regard them as a resting place of the spirits of the dead and as the birthplace of all life. In 2006 Sheila Coulson of the University of Oslo announced that a rock in Rhino Cave resembling a python's head, carved with many cup-shaped hollows and associated with 70,000-year-old artefacts, was evidence of the earliest known human ritual.

alternatives.label: Earliest ritual (Coulson)
alternatives.text: The python-like rock and the cave's images of python, elephant and giraffe – the San's three most important animals – were read as a 70,000-year-old ritual site.

alternatives.label: Critics
alternatives.text: Archaeologists who first investigated the site in 1995–96 pointed out that the cupules are not all the same age (some fresh, some heavily patinated), that over 20 nearby rocks have similar hollows without resembling animals, and that the site's dating does not support 70,000 years.

entries.title: Altamira: cave art dismissed as a forgery
entries.dateNote: Earliest paintings c. 36,000 years ago; most famous polychromes much later
entries.mainstream: In 1879 Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola's eight-year-old daughter María led him to the paintings in the Altamira cave in Cantabria, Spain (found in 1868 by tiler Modesto Cubillas). Sautuola and Juan Vilanova y Piera published them in 1880 as Palaeolithic, but leading French prehistorians such as Gabriel de Mortillet and Émile Cartailhac ridiculed the claim at the 1880 congress in Lisbon, partly because prehistoric people were assumed incapable of such art; Sautuola was accused of hiring a contemporary painter. After similar caves were found in France, Cartailhac published "Mea culpa d'un sceptique" in 1902, 14 years after Sautuola's death. Uranium-series dating (Pike et al. 2012) indicates that the earliest paintings there go back about 36,000 years.

alternatives.label: Forgery accusation (historical)
alternatives.text: Sceptics pointed to the lack of soot on the walls and the paintings' freshness; Sautuola later suggested lamps burning marrow fat would have produced little soot.

alternatives.label: Lesson drawn
alternatives.text: The case is often cited as an example of experts rejecting evidence that conflicted with assumptions about "primitive" ancestors; it also shows the opposite risk, since real forgeries exist (see Piltdown).

entries.changed: 1880: published as Palaeolithic and widely rejected. 1902: Cartailhac's public retraction. 1985: UNESCO World Heritage. 2012: U-series dating pushes the earliest marks back to c. 36,000 years.

entries.title: Ötzi the Iceman
entries.dateNote: Died c. 3275–3230 BCE; found 1991
entries.mainstream: The natural mummy of a man who lived around 3275–3230 BCE, found on 19 September 1991 by hikers Helmut and Erika Simon at about 3,210 m near the Tisenjoch pass in the Ötztal Alps on the Austria–Italy border; at first he was taken for a recently dead mountaineer. He carried a copper axe with a yew handle, a flint knife and a quiver of 14 arrows. In 2001 X-rays revealed a flint arrowhead in his left shoulder; he probably bled to death, and he had cuts on his hands and a head injury. A 2023 genome found about 90% Anatolian-farmer ancestry, likely darker skin than present-day Europeans and probable baldness. He is in the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology, Bolzano.

alternatives.label: Murder on the mountain
alternatives.text: Most researchers think he was killed by another person near where he lay; blood traces of several other people on his gear (2003, disputed) led to scenarios of a fight.

alternatives.label: Burial theory
alternatives.text: A 2010 study (Vanzetti et al.) proposed he died lower down and was ceremonially placed on a stone platform higher up; other researchers argue his intact wound and bones show no sign of being moved.

entries.title: The stone spheres of Costa Rica
entries.dateNote: c. 600–1550 CE (uncertain)
entries.mainstream: More than 300 stone balls on the Diquís Delta and Isla del Caño in southern Costa Rica, attributed to the Diquís culture, ranging from a few centimetres to over 2 metres across and up to 15 tons, mostly carved from gabbro by hammering and sand polishing. They are believed to date from about 600 CE, mostly after 1000 CE and before the Spanish conquest, but dating is hard because most have been moved. Banana-plantation workers of the United Fruit Company uncovered them in the 1930s and, hoping for hidden gold, dynamited some. Doris Stone published the first study in 1943 and Samuel Lothrop surveyed them in 1948. Their settlements became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014.

alternatives.label: Mainstream meaning
alternatives.text: Archaeologists think they were placed in lines along the approach to chiefs' houses; their exact significance is uncertain, and some suggest they represent the sun and moon.

alternatives.label: Atlantis and stone-softening (alternative)
alternatives.text: Popular myths say they came from Atlantis or were made with a potion that softens rock (geopolymer researcher Joseph Davidovits has been cited for this); most spheres are of acid-resistant gabbro.

alternatives.label: "Perfectly round"? (claim examined)
alternatives.text: Claims of near-perfect roundness came from misreading Lothrop's tables, whose three-decimal figures were averages of tape measurements; some spheres vary by over 5 cm in diameter.

sources.title: UNESCO: Precolumbian Chiefdom Settlements with Stone Spheres of the Diquís

entries.title: The iron pillar of Delhi: "the pillar that does not rust"
entries.dateNote: c. 375–415 CE (Chandragupta II); moved to Delhi in the 11th century
entries.mainstream: A 7.21 m iron pillar (1.12 m below ground), 41 cm in diameter and weighing more than six tonnes, now in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli, Delhi. Its oldest Sanskrit inscription, in Gupta script, records a king "Chandra" – generally identified as Chandragupta II (r. c. 375–415 CE) – raising a standard of Vishnu on a hill called Vishnupada. It was probably first set up elsewhere (possibly outside the Udayagiri Caves) and moved to Delhi by Anangpal Tomar in the 11th century. Its famous resistance to corrosion comes from an even protective layer of crystalline iron hydrogen phosphate hydrate forming on its high-phosphorus iron.

alternatives.label: Ancient astronauts (claim and retraction)
alternatives.text: In Chariots of the Gods? (1969) Erich von Däniken cited its lack of corrosion and "unknown" manufacture as evidence of extraterrestrial visitation; told in a 1974 interview that it does rust and that its making is understood, he said he no longer considered it a mystery.

alternatives.label: Metallurgical view
alternatives.text: Materials scientist R. Balasubramaniam called it "a living testimony to the skill of metallurgists of ancient India"; 2009 research found that corrosion has developed evenly over its surface.

entries.title: The Nine Unknown Men of Ashoka
entries.dateNote: Claimed founding c. 270 BCE; first known as a story in 1923
entries.mainstream: A legend of a secret society of nine men guarding nine books of dangerous knowledge. Its best-known form is Talbot Mundy's 1923 adventure novel The Nine Unknown, serialised in Adventure magazine, in which the Nine protect the ancient wisdom of Hindu sages. In their 1960 book The Morning of the Magicians, Louis Pauwels and Jacques Bergier claimed the Nine were real, founded by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka around 270 BCE, that Pope Silvester II had met them, and that the 19th-century French writer Louis Jacolliot had insisted on their existence. No historical source for the society is known; it has since inspired many novels and TV series.

alternatives.label: Real secret society (claim)
alternatives.text: Pauwels and Bergier presented the Nine as a real, ongoing guardianship of suppressed science; later fiction adds knowledge of time travel and contact with extraterrestrials.

alternatives.label: Literary origin
alternatives.text: Mainstream view: the idea is modern literary and esoteric invention, popularised by a novel and an occult bestseller; no historical source for it is known.

entries.title: Jiroft: a lost Bronze Age civilisation in Iran?
entries.dateNote: Heyday c. 2500–2200 BCE
entries.mainstream: An early Bronze Age culture of south-eastern Iran (Kerman and Sistan-Baluchestan), also called the "Intercultural" or Halil Rud style. Before 2001, looters south of Jiroft dug up many carved vessels in the "Intercultural style"; Iranian authorities recovered many, and from 2001 a team led by Yusef Majidzadeh excavated two mounds, Konar Sandal A and B, finding a citadel and over two square kilometres of a city whose heyday was c. 2500–2200 BCE. Majidzadeh proposed an independent civilisation between Elam and the Indus Valley, with its own architecture and language.

alternatives.label: Aratta (Majidzadeh)
alternatives.text: Majidzadeh identified Jiroft with Aratta, the rich land of Sumerian epics; many scholars are sceptical, and others (e.g. Daniel Potts, Piotr Steinkeller) connect Konar Sandal with Marhashi, a state east of Elam.

alternatives.label: Earliest writing? (disputed)
alternatives.text: Inscribed bricks and tablets from Konar Sandal, in a geometric script that Majidzadeh related to Elamite writing, were promoted as possibly the oldest writing; a 2007 Science news article asked "Ancient writing or modern fakery?", reflecting doubts about some objects.

alternatives.label: Criticism
alternatives.text: Oscar Muscarella of the Metropolitan Museum criticised sensational announcements and slow scholarly publication, while still acknowledging the site's importance.

sources.title: Excavations at Konar Sandal in the Region of Jiroft in the Halil Basin: First Preliminary Report (2002–2008)

entries.title: Daisen Kofun: Japan's giant tomb that may not be opened
entries.dateNote: Mid-5th century CE
entries.mainstream: The Daisenryō Kofun in Sakai, Osaka, is the largest of Japan's more than 20,000 burial mounds (3rd–7th centuries): a keyhole-shaped tumulus 486 m long, ringed by moats and thought to have been built over about 20 years in the mid-5th century. It is commonly accepted, though it cannot be confirmed, to be the tomb of Emperor Nintoku, and the Imperial Household Agency treats it as such: the mound is off-limits, overgrown and protected as an imperial mausoleum. It belongs to the Mozu-Furuichi Kofun Group, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2019; more than half of the Mozu mounds were destroyed by post-war housing development.

alternatives.label: Who is buried?
alternatives.text: The identification with Nintoku follows tradition; because the mound is closed as an imperial mausoleum it cannot be tested by excavation.

alternatives.label: Open or closed? (two views)
alternatives.text: Kofun-period finds show close links with the Korean peninsula (shared armour styles, mirrors from the same moulds, immigrant toraijin clans). Some see closed imperial tombs as limiting inquiry into such questions; others see the closure as proper protection of sacred imperial graves.

sources.title: UNESCO: Mozu-Furuichi Kofun Group: Mounded Tombs of Ancient Japan

entries.title: Urashima Tarō: the fisherman who lost 300 years
entries.dateNote: Nihon Shoki dates the voyage to 478 CE; texts from the 8th century
entries.mainstream: A Japanese tale in which a fisherman rescues a turtle and is taken to the palace of the sea-god (in older versions, the land of immortals, Hōrai or Tokoyo). He stays what seems a few days; when he goes home, centuries have passed, and when he opens the forbidden box (tamatebako) the princess gave him, he becomes an old man. It goes back to 8th-century texts: the Tango Province Fudoki, the Man'yōshū and the Nihon Shoki, which places Urashimako's departure in the 22nd year of Emperor Yūryaku (478 CE in Aston's translation). A document at Urashima Jinja shrine says he returned in 825 CE.

alternatives.label: Folklore type
alternatives.text: Folklorists class it with tales of "the relativity of time" (ATU 681), found worldwide, including the Chinese woodcutter Wang Zhi who watches immortals play a game while years pass ("Rotten Axe Handle Mountain"); the Chinese story is sometimes conjectured as a source.

alternatives.label: Modern readings (speculative)
alternatives.text: The motif has been compared with relativistic time dilation (sometimes called the "Urashima effect" in Japan) and with "missing time" in modern abduction narratives; such parallels are modern interpretations, not part of the tale's origin.

entries.title: King Kakudmi: an audience with Brahma while ages pass
entries.dateNote: Undated legend recorded in the Mahabharata, Harivamsha and Puranas
entries.mainstream: In Hindu texts (the Mahabharata, Harivamsha, Vishnu Purana, Devi Bhagavatam and Bhagavata Purana), King Kakudmi (Raivata) of Kushasthali takes his daughter Revati to Brahma's realm to ask which suitor she should marry. They wait while Brahma listens to a musical performance; Brahma then explains that many ages have passed on Earth, and all the suitors and their descendants are long dead. Returning, they find that 27 chaturyugas (about 117 million years) have passed, their city Kushasthali has become Dvaraka, and men have "dwindled in stature"; Revati marries Balarama, brother of Krishna.

alternatives.label: Religious meaning
alternatives.text: Within Hindu cosmology the story illustrates the vast, nested cycles of time (yugas and manvantaras) and the difference between divine and human time.

alternatives.label: Cross-cultural pattern
alternatives.text: It is one of the oldest stories of time passing differently in another realm, alongside Urashima Tarō (Japan) and Oisín in Tír na nÓg (Ireland); writers have compared it with relativistic time dilation, a modern analogy rather than an ancient claim.

entries.title: Kaguya-hime: the princess from the Moon
entries.dateNote: Composed late 9th or early 10th century
entries.mainstream: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter (Taketori Monogatari), by an unknown author of the late 9th or early 10th century, is considered the oldest surviving Japanese monogatari. A bamboo cutter finds a tiny girl in a glowing bamboo stalk; she grows into the beautiful Kaguya-hime, sets impossible tasks for five suitors and refuses the emperor. Finally she reveals she is from the Moon; an embassy of heavenly beings descends, the emperor's guards are blinded by a strange light, and she returns to the Moon. The emperor has her elixir of immortality burned on the mountain closest to heaven – one legend of the name of Mount Fuji (fushi, "immortality"). The oldest surviving manuscript dates from 1592.

alternatives.label: Literary and religious roots
alternatives.text: Scholars relate it to Chinese tales such as Chang'e, who fled to the Moon with the elixir of immortality, and to Daoist and Buddhist ideas of immortals and celestial realms.

alternatives.label: Visitor from the sky (modern reading, speculative)
alternatives.text: Some modern readers describe the descending heavenly host and blinding light as resembling a UFO encounter and Kaguya as an extraterrestrial; this is a modern interpretation of a court romance.

entries.title: Kailasa temple, Ellora: a temple carved from the top down
entries.dateNote: Mainly 8th century CE (Krishna I, r. c. 756–773)
entries.mainstream: The largest of the 34 Hindu, Buddhist and Jain rock-cut temples and monasteries at Ellora, Maharashtra (UNESCO World Heritage). The Kailasa temple (Cave 16) is a monolith cut out of the basalt cliff, carved vertically from the top of the rock downward; its sanctuary rises 32.6 m above the court. It has no dedicatory inscription, but copper-plate grants of c. 812–813 CE credit "Krishnaraja", generally identified as the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I (r. c. 756–773), with a temple so wondrous that "even the gods and the architect were astonished".

alternatives.label: Legend of a temple in a week
alternatives.text: A medieval Marathi legend (Katha-Kalpataru, c. 1470–1535) says a queen vowed to fast until she saw a temple's top; the architect Kokasa finished the shikhara in a week by carving from the top. M. K. Dhavalikar suggests Kokasa may really have been the chief architect.

alternatives.label: How long did it take?
alternatives.text: Dhavalikar estimated that 250 labourers cutting about 4 cubic feet each per day could finish it in about 5.5 years, and that quarrying a monolith is less work than hauling stone; others think its mixed styles show work over several reigns.

alternatives.label: Lost-technology claims (speculative)
alternatives.text: Popular alternative-history media sometimes claim such a monolith required lost advanced technology; archaeologists see no need for this, pointing to the inscriptions, labour estimates and comparable temples such as the Virupaksha at Pattadakal.

entries.title: Shambhala, the hidden kingdom
entries.dateNote: Kalachakra tradition from the 11th century; prophesied battle in 2424/2425
entries.mainstream: A spiritual kingdom in Tibetan Buddhist tradition, described in the Kalachakra ("Wheel of Time") tantra, which reached Tibet in the 11th century; the Bon religion has a similar land, Olmo Lung Ring. The name comes from a city in the Hindu Puranas, where the Vishnu Purana prophesies Shambhala as the birthplace of Kalki, who will begin a new golden age. The Kalachakra prophesies that when the world sinks into war and greed, the 25th Kalki king will ride out of Shambhala with a great army, in a final battle dated to 2424 or 2425, followed by a golden age.

alternatives.label: Spiritual reading
alternatives.text: Some Buddhist teachers interpret Shambhala as a pure land or state of mind reached through practice rather than a place on a map.

alternatives.label: Physical hidden land (searches)
alternatives.text: Nicholas and Helena Roerich led expeditions (1924–28, 1934–35), believing Belukha Mountain in the Altai to be an entrance; in the 1920s Soviet secret-police cryptographer Gleb Bokii and Alexander Barchenko planned an expedition to retrieve its wisdom. Alexandra David-Néel linked it with Balkh in Afghanistan.

alternatives.label: Esoteric versions
alternatives.text: Theosophical and neo-Theosophical writers such as Alice Bailey made it the seat of a hidden brotherhood of masters guiding humanity; it influenced the fictional Shangri-La.

entries.title: The Yeti ("Abominable Snowman")
entries.dateNote: Folklore older; Western name from 1921
entries.mainstream: A large, hairy, ape-like creature said to live in the Himalayas. The English name "Abominable Snowman" dates from the 1921 British Everest reconnaissance led by Charles Howard-Bury, who reported footprints at about 6,400 m. Interest peaked after Eric Shipton photographed large prints in 1951 and Hillary and Tenzing reported footprints in 1953. Monastery "Yeti scalps" (Pangboche, Khumjung) were examined by Hillary's 1960–61 expedition. DNA studies have repeatedly matched alleged Yeti hair, bone and scat to bears.

alternatives.label: Unknown primate (cryptozoology)
alternatives.text: Believers point to consistent Sherpa and Tibetan accounts (several named kinds, such as migoi, "wild man"), footprint casts and photographs as evidence of an undiscovered ape.

alternatives.label: Bears (genetic studies)
alternatives.text: Sykes et al. (2014) matched two Himalayan samples to an ancient polar-bear sequence and suggested a hybrid bear; later work (2015) found brown bear more likely, and Lan et al. (2017) identified most "Yeti" samples as Himalayan or Tibetan brown bears or Asian black bear, and one as a domestic dog. Daniel C. Taylor (2017) argues the Asian black bear explains classic footprints.

alternatives.label: Folklore view
alternatives.text: Folklorists trace the Yeti to Sherpa folklore plus misidentified animals; the Tibetan root word appears to mean "rock bear".

entries.title: The Mongolian death worm (olgoi-khorkhoi)
entries.dateNote: Described 1922; publicised 1926
entries.mainstream: A cryptid of Mongolian folklore said to live in the Gobi Desert: sausage-shaped, about two feet long, headless and legless, and so poisonous that touching it means instant death, according to a description by Mongolian prime minister Damdinbazar in 1922. It reached the West through Roy Chapman Andrews's 1926 book On the Trail of Ancient Man; Andrews himself did not believe in it. Later tales say it can kill at a distance with venom or electric shocks. In 1983, locals who claimed to have seen it identified a Tartar sand boa as the same animal.

alternatives.label: Undiscovered animal (cryptozoology)
alternatives.text: Searchers, from Ivan Mackerle (1990, 1992, using a motorised "thumper" inspired by Dune) to Richard Freeman (2005) and TV teams, found nothing; Freeman concluded the powers were apocryphal but that sightings might involve an unknown worm lizard.

alternatives.label: Folklore and known animals
alternatives.text: Mainstream view: a legend built on misidentified real animals such as the sand boa, amplified by retelling; palaeontologist Ivan Yefremov heard the legend many times in the 1940s but met no one who had seen it.

entries.title: The Baigong "pipes" of Qinghai
entries.mainstream: Pipe-like structures in and around White Mountain (Baigongshan), about 40 km south-west of Delingha in Qinghai, China, found in and near a cave and along the shore of Lake Toson. They became famous through Chinese newspaper reports in June 2002, which described "rusty" iron pipes; a local smeltery analysis reported about 30% iron oxide with much silica and calcium oxide. A 2003 report said Chinese scientists had found organic plant material and tree rings in them, so they were judged to be fossilised trees or roots; the local government promotes them as a tourist attraction.

alternatives.label: Artificial pipes (popular claim)
alternatives.text: Media and alternative writers presented them as ancient or non-human iron plumbing, sometimes linked to an extraterrestrial base; this view relies on the pipe-like shape and iron content.

alternatives.label: Natural formations
alternatives.text: Mainstream explanation: iron-rich concretions formed around fossil tree roots; the oxide analysis is consistent with natural minerals such as calcite and iron oxides.
